sciXsTrack: Which ramp makes a toy car go the slowest?
A low, gentle ramp
A tall, steep ramp
A very tall ramp
A ramp as steep as a slide
A gentle ramp gives the car less speed than a steep one.
Your toy car crashes hard at the bottom of the ramp. What could slow it down safely?
Put a soft towel at the end
Make the ramp taller
Push the car harder
Make the track smoother
A soft towel adds friction and cushions the car so it stops gently.
Which surface slows a toy car down the most?
Thick carpet
Smooth wood
A tile floor
A plastic track
Thick carpet has a lot of friction, so it slows the car the most.
Your track has a big gap in it. What should you do?
Fill the gap with another piece of track
Make the gap bigger so cars can jump
Paint the track a brighter colour
Use a heavier car that rolls faster
Filling the gap lets the car keep rolling without falling.
What is a good first step before you build a race car track?
Draw a plan of the track
Knock over the blocks
Race the cars right away
Hide the materials
Engineers plan their design before they build it.
You want to know which of two cars is faster. How can you make the race fair?
Race both cars on the same ramp
Use a steeper ramp for one car
Push one car harder
Start one car higher up
Using the same ramp for both cars means only the cars are different.
A track that lets a car go around and come back to the start is shaped like a…
loop
straight line
dead end
single ramp
A loop goes around and returns to where it started.
What could you use to build a ramp for a toy car?
A flat piece of cardboard
A cotton ball
A pillow
A sock
Cardboard is flat and stiff, so a car can roll down it.
What happens when a toy car starts from higher up on a ramp?
It goes faster and farther
It stops right away
It goes slower
It rolls backward
Starting higher gives the car more speed as it rolls down.
Your car stops in the middle of the track. How can you help it go all the way?
Start it from higher on the ramp
Put sand on the track
Make the ramp flatter
Put carpet on the track
A higher start gives the car more speed so it rolls farther.
Which kind of wheels helps a toy car roll best on a track?
Round wheels that spin
Square wheels
No wheels at all
Wheels glued so they cannot turn
Round wheels that spin freely let the car roll easily.
Your car flies off the track at a sharp turn. What could you change?
Make the turn wider and gentler
Make the ramp steeper
Push the car harder
Take away the sides of the track
A wider, gentler turn helps the car stay on the track.
How can you tell which car rolled the farthest?
Measure with a measuring tape
Guess by looking at the colours
Ask the car
Count the wheels
Measuring the distance gives a fair answer.
One track is smooth and one is bumpy. On which track will a car slow down more?
The bumpy track
The smooth track
Both the same
Neither track
Bumps create more friction and slow the car down.
What could you use to hold up one end of a ramp?
A stack of books
A sheet of paper
A balloon
A puddle of water
A stack of books is strong and steady enough to raise a ramp.
Your friend's track design works better than yours. What should you do?
Look at their design and try their ideas
Knock their track down so yours wins
Give up and stop building your track
Hide their track so nobody sees it
Engineers learn from other designs to improve their own.
Why should you test your track more than one time?
To check that the result is the same each time
To wear the track out a little faster
To make the track look a lot dirtier
To make the toy cars tired from racing
Testing many times shows whether the results can be trusted.
Which part of a track could make a toy car jump?
A small ramp that tilts up at the end
A long strip of soft, bumpy carpet
A tall wall standing across the track
A flat stopping spot at the very end
A ramp that tilts up launches the car into the air.
Which tool helps you time a toy car race?
A stopwatch
A ruler
A thermometer
A magnifying glass
A stopwatch measures how long the car takes to finish.
Your ramp keeps sliding when the car rolls down. How can you fix it?
Tape the ramp so it stays in place
Pour some water on the ramp first
Put round marbles under the ramp
Make the ramp much taller and steeper
Tape holds the ramp steady so it does not slide.
Which track would make a toy car go the fastest?
A steep, smooth track
A flat, carpeted track
A gentle, bumpy track
A flat, sandy track
Steepness adds speed and smoothness means less friction.
Your toy car keeps tipping over on the track. What could help?
Make the track wider and flatter
Make the track bumpier
Push the car harder
Make the ramp steeper
A wide, flat track gives the car a steady path.

sciEngDP: Which step of the engineering-design process is this? Students learn that a classroom gets too hot and they need a cheap way to shade the windows.
Identifying the need and limits is defining the problem.

Coming up with many possible ideas is brainstorming.
Which step of the engineering-design process is this? Students glue straws and tape together to make their first model bridge.
Making a first working model is building a prototype.
Which step of the engineering-design process is this? Students time how long their paper helicopter takes to fall 2 m.
Measuring how well a design works is testing.

Changing a design after testing is improving it.

Setting the requirements and limits is part of defining the problem.

Sketching several possible designs is brainstorming.

A first physical model is a prototype.

Which step of the engineering-design process is this? The class builds a cardboard model of a playground slide.

sciMCH: Which simple machine is a doorknob?

sciXsETrans: A battery-powered fan changes chemical energy into…
The battery's chemical energy becomes electricity, which spins the fan's motor.
An electric kettle changes electrical energy into…
The kettle's heating element turns electricity into heat that boils the water.
A microphone changes sound energy into…
A microphone turns sound vibrations into electrical signals.
A campfire changes the chemical energy in wood into…
Burning wood releases stored chemical energy as heat and light.
An electric motor changes electrical energy into…
A motor uses electricity to make something spin or move.
A hydroelectric dam changes the kinetic energy of falling water into…
Falling water spins turbines connected to generators that make electricity.
A doorbell changes electrical energy into…
Pressing the button sends electricity to the bell, which makes sound.
A battery being charged changes electrical energy into…
Charging stores energy in the battery as chemical energy.
A glow stick changes chemical energy into…
Chemicals inside a glow stick react and give off light.
A hand-crank flashlight changes kinetic energy into…
Turning the crank spins a generator, and the electricity powers the bulb.
A drum changes the kinetic energy of the drumstick into…
Hitting the drum makes it vibrate, which produces sound.
A ball held high and then dropped changes gravitational potential energy into…
As the ball falls, its stored energy of height turns into motion.
An electric stove changes electrical energy into…
The stove's burners turn electricity into heat for cooking.
A stretched elastic band changes elastic potential energy into…
kinetic energy when it is let go
The stored energy in the stretched band turns into motion when released.
A television changes electrical energy into…
A TV uses electricity to make pictures (light) and sound.
A bicycle's brakes change kinetic energy into…
Friction between brake pads and the wheel turns motion into heat.
A natural gas furnace changes chemical energy into…
Burning natural gas releases heat that warms a home.
A firefly changes chemical energy into…
Chemical reactions in a firefly's body produce light.
A swinging pendulum keeps changing energy between…
At the top it has the most potential energy, and at the bottom it has the most kinetic energy.
A roller coaster going down a hill changes potential energy into…
As the car drops, its stored energy of height becomes speed.
A phone's speaker changes electrical energy into…
The speaker uses electricity to vibrate and make sound.
When you lift a backpack onto a shelf, your muscles change chemical energy into…
kinetic energy and then gravitational potential energy
Your muscles use food energy to move the backpack, which gains stored energy from its height.

sciEnTrans: A gas stove heats a pot of water. What energy change happens in the flame?
Burning gas releases stored chemical energy as heat (thermal energy).

The fan's motor turns electrical energy into the kinetic energy of the spinning blades.

Photosynthesis stores the energy of sunlight as chemical energy in sugar.

Moving water spins turbines, and the generator turns that kinetic energy into electrical energy.

The doorbell uses electrical energy to make sound.

A microphone turns sound vibrations into electrical signals.

sciWTR: Wet laundry on a clothesline dries in the sun. What process is this?

Water gathering in lakes, rivers and oceans is collection.

Groundwater fills the spaces in soil and rock below the surface.
What happens to water vapour as it rises high into the sky?

It falls straight back as vapour

Rain picks salt out of the air

What is the correct order in this part of the water cycle?

Snow changing directly into water vapour on a sunny, dry, cold day is called …

Why is the water cycle important to living things?

It makes the oceans saltier for animals
It creates new water from nothing

Which part of the water cycle would happen faster on a hot, windy day?

a cloud that forms close to the ground

The height of each plant

To change the results later
To skip measuring

The water temperature
The pot size

Change the numbers
Throw away the data

Plant height
The amount of soil

A few minutes
One hour
One second

Why should the student label each pot?

To make the pots heavier and steadier
To help the plants grow faster in sunlight

A ruler
A thermometer
A balance

A stopwatch
A ruler
A graduated cylinder

Which tool should be used to measure the same volume of water for each cup?
A graduated cylinder
A thermometer
A stopwatch
A ruler

A student tests whether the size of a sugar cube affects how fast it dissolves and spreads. What is the independent variable?

The time to dissolve
The water temperature

So the dye looks brighter
So the water heats faster
So the experiment is shorter

Drink the coloured water

A pie chart of the three dye colours

To use up the dye
To change the temperature
To make the water colder

evaporation
condensation
melting

Solid
Liquid
Frozen solid

Which change would SLOW DOWN diffusion of food colouring in water?

Using warmer water
Stirring the water
Shaking the cup

conclusion
control
procedure

To hold in the Moon's oxygen
To make the habitat float
Without an atmosphere, the Moon's surface is exposed to radiation and micrometeorites.
Why do solar panels work well for power on most of the Moon's surface?
Sunlight is not blocked by clouds or air
The Moon makes its own sunlight
The Moon is always in daylight
Solar panels need no sunlight on the Moon
With no atmosphere, sunlight reaches the surface directly, though long lunar nights still need stored power.
A night on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks. What design problem does this create?
Equipment needs stored power and heat to survive
Astronauts cannot sleep for two weeks
Rovers must drive twice as fast
Solar panels make too much power
During the long, cold lunar night there is no sunlight, so batteries and heaters are needed.
Why do engineers brainstorm many ideas before choosing one?
Considering many ideas makes a better solution more likely
It is required to use all the ideas
Brainstorming replaces testing
The first idea is always the worst
Generating several possible solutions helps engineers find the one that best fits the criteria.
A spacecraft must fit inside the nose cone of a rocket. This is an example of a…
size constraint
test result
scientific law
prototype
The nose cone sets a limit on the spacecraft's size, so it is a constraint.
Why would engineers reuse water on a Moon base?
Water is heavy to bring from Earth and scarce on the Moon
Water on the Moon is too salty
Reusing water makes it heavier
Astronauts do not need water
Recycling water reduces how much must be launched from Earth.
How do Moon landers slow down before touching down?
They fire rocket engines downward
They open large parachutes
They glide on wings through the air
They bounce off the clouds
With no air for parachutes or wings, landers use rocket engines to slow their fall.
Why are lunar spacesuits tested in vacuum chambers on Earth?
A vacuum chamber copies the airless conditions on the Moon
Vacuum chambers make suits lighter
Vacuum chambers add Moon gravity
Spacesuits are cleaned in vacuum chambers
Testing in a vacuum lets engineers check that suits work in conditions like the Moon's.
A rover keeps getting stuck in sand during a test. What is the best next step?
Change the wheel design and test again
Launch the rover to the Moon anyway
Stop testing because it failed once
Paint the rover a lighter colour
Engineers use test failures to improve the design and then retest it.
Why do engineers communicate with the public and other teams about a Moon mission?
To share results, gain feedback and support
To keep the mission a total secret
Because talking replaces engineering
To change the laws of physics
Sharing designs and results helps teams improve ideas and keeps the public informed.
Why can radio messages from the Moon reach Earth, but sound cannot?
Radio waves travel through space, but sound needs matter
Sound is too slow to leave the Moon
Radio waves need air to travel
The Moon blocks all sound waves
Sound needs a medium such as air, but radio waves can travel through the vacuum of space.
Which is a trade-off in designing a Moon rover?
Adding more batteries gives more range but adds mass
Bigger wheels always make it lighter
Adding cameras removes the need for power
Painting it white makes it faster
A trade-off means improving one feature makes another worse, like range versus mass.
Why do Moon missions often send robots before people?
Robots can explore safely and gather data first
Robots are always cheaper than paper
People are not allowed to visit the Moon
Robots can breathe Moon air
Robotic missions reduce risk by scouting conditions before humans arrive.
sciXsAbForce: What is the symbol for watt (power)?
The watt, the unit of power, uses the symbol W.
What is the symbol for coulomb (electric charge)?
The coulomb, the unit of charge, uses the symbol C.
What is the symbol for kilojoule?
The prefix kilo is a lowercase k, and joule is a capital J.
What is the symbol for kilowatt?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and watt uses a capital W.
What is the symbol for milliampere?
Milli uses a lowercase m and ampere uses a capital A.
What is the symbol for kilonewton?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and newton uses a capital N.
What is the symbol for kilovolt?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and volt uses a capital V.
What is the symbol for megawatt?
Mega uses a capital M, and watt uses a capital W; mW would mean milliwatt.
What is the symbol for millivolt?
Milli uses a lowercase m; MV would mean megavolt.
What is the symbol for kilowatt-hour (electrical energy)?
A kilowatt-hour is written kWh: lowercase k, capital W, lowercase h.
What is the symbol for megajoule?
Mega uses a capital M and joule uses a capital J.
What is the symbol for kilohm?
Kilo uses a lowercase k and ohm uses the Greek letter omega, Ω.
Which unit does the symbol N stand for?
N is the symbol for the newton, the SI unit of force.
Which unit does the symbol J stand for?
J is the symbol for the joule, the SI unit of energy.
Which unit does the symbol W stand for?
W is the symbol for the watt, the SI unit of power.
Which unit does the symbol V stand for?
V is the symbol for the volt, the SI unit of electric potential difference.
Which unit does the symbol A stand for?
A is the symbol for the ampere, the SI unit of electric current.
Which unit does the symbol Ω stand for?
Ω is the symbol for the ohm, the SI unit of electrical resistance.
Which unit does the symbol C stand for?
In electricity, C is the symbol for the coulomb, the unit of charge.
Which is the correct way to write 5 kilowatts?
The kilo prefix is a lowercase k, and units named after people use a capital letter.
Which is the correct way to write 250 milliamperes?
Milli is a lowercase m and ampere is a capital A.

The newton's symbol is a single capital N.
sciDensCmp: Gold has a density of 19.3 g/cm³ and aluminum has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Which is denser?
Gold has the greater mass per cubic centimetre, so it is denser.
A wooden block (0.6 g/cm³) is placed in water (1.0 g/cm³). What happens?
An object less dense than water floats.
Two balls are the same size. Ball X has a mass of 50 g and Ball Y has a mass of 20 g. Which is denser?
With equal volumes, the one with more mass is denser.
Two objects have the same mass. Object P has a volume of 10 cm³ and Object Q has a volume of 40 cm³. Which is denser?
The same mass packed into a smaller volume means greater density.
Honey (1.4 g/cm³), water (1.0 g/cm³) and vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³) are poured into a jar. Which layer ends up on the bottom?
The densest liquid sinks to the bottom.
Honey (1.4 g/cm³), water (1.0 g/cm³) and vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³) are poured into a jar. Which layer ends up on top?
The least dense liquid floats on top.
A plastic toy sinks in water but floats in salt water. What does this tell you?
Salt water is denser than fresh water
Fresh water is denser than salt water
The toy got lighter in salt water
Salt water and fresh water are equally dense
An object floats in a liquid denser than itself, so salt water must be denser than fresh water.
A steel nail sinks in water, but a large steel ship floats. Why?
The ship's hollow shape gives it a lower overall density
The ship is made of lighter steel
The ship has less mass than the nail
The ship encloses lots of air, so its average density is less than water.
Which is denser: 1 kg of feathers or 1 kg of iron?
They have the same mass, but iron takes up much less volume, so it is denser.
A piece of clay is rolled into a long snake shape. What happens to its density?
Changing the shape does not change the mass or volume, so density stays the same.
Mercury has a density of 13.6 g/cm³. Would a steel bolt (7.8 g/cm³) sink or float in mercury?
Steel is less dense than mercury, so it floats on mercury.
Granite is 2.7 g/cm³ and pumice is 0.6 g/cm³. Which rock could float on water?
Pumice is less dense than water (1.0 g/cm³), so it can float; granite sinks.
A grape sinks in water. What can you say about its density?
It is the same as air
Objects that sink in water are denser than water's 1.0 g/cm³.
Hot air rises above cool air. Which is less dense?
Heated air expands, so its density decreases and it rises.
Substance A: 30 g in 10 cm³. Substance B: 30 g in 15 cm³. Which is denser?
A has a density of 3 g/cm³ and B has 2 g/cm³, so A is denser.
Substance A: 12 g in 4 cm³. Substance B: 20 g in 10 cm³. Which is denser?
A is 3 g/cm³ and B is 2 g/cm³, so A is denser even though B has more mass.
A small pebble sinks in water, but a large log floats. Which statement is correct?
The pebble is denser than the log
The log is denser than the pebble
The pebble has more mass than the log
Sinking or floating depends on density, not size, so the pebble is denser.
A block of ice (0.92 g/cm³) is placed in vegetable oil (0.9 g/cm³). What happens?
Ice is slightly denser than vegetable oil, so it sinks in oil.
A cube of copper is cut into four smaller pieces. How does the density of each piece compare to the original?
It is one quarter as much
Density is a property of the substance, so it does not change when the sample is cut.
Which material is the least dense? Lead 11.3 g/cm³, aluminum 2.7 g/cm³, iron 7.9 g/cm³, cork 0.24 g/cm³
Cork has the smallest density of the four.
Which material is the most dense? Silver 10.5 g/cm³, glass 2.5 g/cm³, ice 0.92 g/cm³, oak wood 0.75 g/cm³
Silver has the largest density of the four materials.
Why does a helium balloon rise in the air?
Helium is less dense than air
Helium has no mass at all
A gas less dense than the surrounding air rises.
sciAccel: Which object is accelerating?
A skateboarder speeding up down a hill
A book resting on a desk
A car moving at a steady 50 km/h in a straight line
A ship sailing straight at a constant speed
Speeding up is a change in velocity, so the skateboarder is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
An elevator rising at a constant speed
A car turning a corner
A ball slowing as it rolls on grass
A sled speeding up down a hill
Constant speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing.
Which object is accelerating?
A Ferris wheel seat moving in a circle at constant speed
A lamp sitting on a table
A plane flying straight at constant speed
A train stopped at a station
Moving in a circle changes direction constantly, so the seat is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
A hockey puck gliding straight at a steady speed on smooth ice
A puck that is slowed by a stick
A puck hit so it speeds up
A puck that bounces off the boards
A puck moving at a constant speed in a straight line has constant velocity.
A cyclist brakes and slows down. Is the cyclist accelerating?
Yes, because the speed is changing
No, because the cyclist is slowing down
No, because the direction is the same
Yes, because the cyclist is moving
Any change in speed, including slowing down, is acceleration.
A car drives around a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its direction is changing
No, because its speed is constant
No, because 30 km/h is slow
Yes, because its speed is increasing

A rock rests on the ground. Is it accelerating?
No, because its velocity is not changing
Yes, because gravity pulls on it
Yes, because Earth is under it
No, because rocks have no mass
An object at rest with balanced forces has a constant velocity of zero.
A soccer ball is kicked and leaves the ground. At the moment of the kick, is the ball accelerating?
Yes, because its speed increases quickly
No, because the foot stops touching it
No, because it was not moving before
Yes, because it is on the ground
The kick changes the ball's speed from zero, which is acceleration.
A rocket lifts off and goes faster and faster. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its speed is increasing
No, because it moves straight up
No, because rockets move at constant speed
Yes, because it is very heavy
Increasing speed means the rocket's velocity is changing.
A ball is thrown straight up and slows as it rises. Is it accelerating?
Yes, because its speed is decreasing
No, because it is going up
No, because it has not stopped yet
Yes, because it is getting heavier
Gravity slows the ball, changing its velocity, so it accelerates.
A truck travels on a straight highway at a steady 100 km/h. Is it accelerating?
No, because its speed and direction are constant
Yes, because 100 km/h is fast
Yes, because the engine is running
No, because trucks cannot accelerate
Constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration.
Which object is accelerating?
A swing slowing down as it reaches the top
A parked car on a flat street
A box sitting on a shelf
A cruise ship sailing straight at steady speed
The swing's speed is changing, so it is accelerating.
Which object is NOT accelerating?
A drone hovering in one place
A drone speeding up as it climbs
A drone turning in a circle
A drone slowing to land
A hovering drone stays still, so its velocity does not change.
A child on a merry-go-round moves at a steady speed. Why is the child accelerating?
The child's direction keeps changing
The child's speed keeps increasing
The child is not moving at all
The child's mass keeps changing
Circular motion means a constant change in direction, which is acceleration.
A runner keeps a steady pace along a straight track. What is the runner's acceleration?
It is zero
It is increasing
It equals the speed
It is decreasing
With no change in speed or direction, the acceleration is zero.
A car's speedometer reads 60 km/h, then 70 km/h, then 80 km/h on a straight road. What is the car doing?
Accelerating by speeding up
Moving at constant velocity
Accelerating by turning
Decelerating as it slows
The speed is increasing, so the car is accelerating.
A car's speedometer stays at 60 km/h as it follows a curved road. What is the car doing?
Accelerating by changing direction
Moving at constant velocity
Accelerating by speeding up
Standing still on the road
Following a curve changes direction, so the car accelerates even at constant speed.
Which change does NOT count as acceleration?
Moving the same speed in the same direction
Speeding up
Slowing down
Changing direction
Acceleration is any change in speed or direction, so no change means no acceleration.
A skydiver falls at a steady terminal speed. Is the skydiver accelerating?
No, because the speed and direction are constant
Yes, because the skydiver is falling
Yes, because gravity always accelerates
No, because the skydiver is not moving
At terminal speed, air resistance balances gravity, so velocity stays constant.
A hockey player skates around the net in a curve without changing speed. Is the player accelerating?
Yes, because the direction is changing
No, because the speed stays the same
No, because ice has no friction
Yes, because the speed is increasing
A change in direction is a change in velocity, so it is acceleration.
A subway train pulls into a station and comes to a stop. Is it accelerating while it stops?
Yes, because its speed is decreasing
No, because it is stopping
No, because it travels underground
Yes, because its direction is reversing
Slowing down is a change in velocity, so the train accelerates.
The Moon orbits Earth. Is the Moon accelerating?
Yes, because its direction keeps changing
No, because it is far from Earth
No, because space has no air
Yes, because it is speeding up forever
Moving in a curved orbit means the Moon's direction, and so its velocity, is always changing.
sciNewton: A person steps off a small boat onto a dock. What happens to the boat?
The boat moves away from the dock
The boat moves toward the dock
The boat stays perfectly still
The boat sinks straight down
The person pushes the boat backward as they push themselves forward, so the boat moves the other way.
A cannon fires a cannonball forward. What happens to the cannon?
It recoils backward
It moves forward with the ball
It stays completely still
It lifts straight upward
The cannon pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes the cannon backward with an equal force.
You push on a box with 30 N. How hard does the box push on you?
30 N, in the opposite direction
30 N, in the same direction
15 N, in the opposite direction
0 N, because boxes cannot push
Newton's third law says forces come in equal and opposite pairs.
A balloon is let go and air rushes out of the back. Which way does the balloon move?
Forward, away from the escaping air
Backward, with the escaping air
Straight down to the floor
It does not move at all

A person walks forward. Which way do their feet push on the ground?
Backward
Forward
Upward only
They do not push
Your feet push the ground backward, and the ground pushes you forward.
A book rests on a table. The book pushes down on the table. What does the table do?
Pushes up on the book with an equal force
Pushes down on the book
Pulls the book sideways
Does nothing to the book
The table exerts an equal and opposite upward force on the book.
A canoeist pushes the paddle backward through the water. What does the water do?
Pushes the canoe forward
Pushes the canoe backward
Pulls the canoe down
Stops the canoe from moving
The water pushes forward on the paddle, moving the canoe forward.
A small car and a large truck collide. Which feels the larger force?
Both feel forces of the same size
The small car feels a larger force
The large truck feels a larger force
Neither vehicle feels any force
By Newton's third law, the forces are equal and opposite, though the car accelerates more.
Two skaters stand face to face and push off each other. What happens?
They both move apart in opposite directions
Only the stronger skater moves
They both move in the same direction
Neither skater moves at all
Each skater pushes the other, so both receive a force in opposite directions.
A jet engine pushes hot gas backward. What does the gas do to the plane?
Pushes the plane forward
Pushes the plane backward
Pulls the plane down
Has no effect on the plane
The gas pushes back on the engine with an equal and opposite force, moving the plane forward.
A fish pushes water backward with its tail. What does the water do?
Pushes the fish forward
Pushes the fish backward
Pulls the fish to the bottom
Nothing at all
The water pushes the fish forward with an equal and opposite force.
A soccer player kicks a ball. What does the ball do to the player's foot?
Pushes back on the foot with equal force
Pulls the foot forward
Pushes the foot with a smaller force
Exerts no force on the foot
The ball exerts a force on the foot equal in size and opposite in direction.
A rifle is fired. Why does it push back against the shooter's shoulder?
The bullet pushes back on the rifle as the rifle pushes it forward
The rifle gets heavier when fired
Air pulls the rifle backward
The shoulder pushes the rifle forward
The forces on the bullet and the rifle are an equal and opposite pair.
A swimmer pushes off the wall of a pool. What pushes the swimmer forward?
The wall pushing on the swimmer
The swimmer pushing on the wall
The water pulling the swimmer
Gravity pulling the swimmer
The swimmer pushes the wall, and the wall pushes the swimmer forward.
A garden hose sprays water forward. What happens to the nozzle?
It is pushed backward
It is pushed forward
It is pulled downward
It feels no force
The water is pushed out forward, so the water pushes the nozzle backward.
Earth pulls the Moon toward it with gravity. What does the Moon do to Earth?
Pulls Earth toward the Moon with an equal force
Pushes Earth away from it
Pulls Earth with a much smaller force
Exerts no force on Earth

A person on roller skates throws a heavy ball forward. What happens to the person?
They roll backward
They roll forward
They stay still
They spin in a circle
The person pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes the person backward.
A hockey stick hits a puck with a force of 40 N. What force does the puck exert on the stick?
40 N, in the opposite direction
40 N, in the same direction
20 N, in the opposite direction
80 N, in the opposite direction
The puck pushes back on the stick with an equal and opposite force.
A squid shoots water out of its body backward. What happens to the squid?
It moves forward
It moves backward
It sinks
It stops moving
Pushing water backward makes the water push the squid forward.
A helicopter's blades push air downward. What does the air do?
Pushes the helicopter upward
Pushes the helicopter downward
Pulls the helicopter sideways
Does nothing to the helicopter
The air pushes back up on the blades, lifting the helicopter.
You lean against a tree and push on it. Why don't you fall into the tree?
The tree pushes back on you with an equal force
The tree pulls you toward it
You stop pushing as you lean
Gravity stops working on you
The tree exerts an equal and opposite force that supports you.
A bowling ball hits a pin. Compared with the force the ball exerts on the pin, the force the pin exerts on the ball is…
equal and opposite
larger and opposite
smaller and in the same direction
zero

sciXsCarSafe: Why do air bags inflate so quickly in a crash?
They must be in place before the person moves forward
They must make a loud warning noise before the crash
They must cool the engine before it overheats
They must lock the wheels so the car stops sooner

Why are side-curtain air bags useful?
They protect the head in side impacts and rollovers
They help the driver see cars behind in the next lane
They keep the side windows clean in rainy weather
They make the car lighter so it can brake faster
Side-curtain air bags cushion the head when the car is hit from the side or rolls over.
What should happen to a seat belt after a serious crash?
It should be replaced
It should be washed
It should be tightened
It should be painted
A seat belt that has stretched in a crash may not protect as well next time.
Why is it dangerous to place a rear-facing infant seat in front of an active air bag?
The inflating air bag can hit the seat with great force
The air bag will not inflate when a baby seat is there
The baby will get too warm from the dashboard heater
The car's engine will not start with a baby seat there
Air bags inflate very forcefully, which can seriously injure a baby close to the dashboard.
Why do car crashes at higher speeds cause more damage?
The car has much more kinetic energy to absorb
The car becomes lighter at high speed
Seat belts stop working at high speed
Air bags inflate too slowly

Why does a seat belt cross the hips and chest instead of the stomach?
Bones there can handle the stopping force better
The stomach is too far from the door
The belt looks better there
The chest is lighter than the stomach
The pelvis and rib cage are strong and spread the force, while the soft stomach can be injured.
What is the job of the rigid passenger cage in a car?
To keep its shape and protect the people inside
To crumple as much as possible and absorb the crash
To hold the engine in place during the whole trip
To make the car lighter so it uses less fuel
The strong passenger compartment resists crushing while crumple zones absorb energy.
Why do booster seats help children who are too small for adult seat belts?
They raise the child so the belt fits across the hips and chest
They let the child see out the window during the trip
They make the seat softer so the ride is more comfy
They keep the child warmer on cold winter mornings
A booster positions the belt over strong bones instead of the neck and stomach.
According to Newton's first law, what happens to a cup of coffee in a cup holder when a car turns sharply?
It tends to keep moving in a straight line
It moves into the turn with the car
It stops moving instantly
It floats upward
Objects keep their motion unless a force changes it, so the coffee resists the turn.
Why are dashboards often padded?
Padding increases stopping time and reduces force on the body
Padding makes the car faster by lowering its total mass
Padding keeps the engine cool by blocking heat from it
Padding helps the radio work by blocking outside noise
Softer surfaces slow a body more gradually, reducing the force of impact.
Why do bumpers absorb small impacts?
To reduce damage in low-speed collisions
To make the car look longer
To hold the licence plate
To make the car brake faster
Bumpers are designed to absorb energy from minor bumps and protect the car's body.
Why does increasing the stopping time in a crash reduce injuries?
The same change in momentum over more time needs less force
It makes the car heavier so it is harder to push
It removes all of the car's momentum instantly
It increases the car's speed so the crash ends sooner
Spreading the change in motion over a longer time lowers the force on the passengers.
Why do engineers use crash-test dummies?
To measure forces on the body safely in crash tests
To drive cars on real roads
To replace seat belts in cars
To make crashes happen faster
Dummies have sensors that record forces in a crash without risking real people.
Why is stopping distance longer on icy roads?
There is less friction between the tires and road
Ice makes the car heavier
Ice increases the brake force
Cold air pushes the car forward
Less friction means the tires cannot slow the car as quickly.
Why should heavy objects be secured in a car's trunk or cargo area?
Loose objects keep moving in a crash and can hit people
Heavy objects slow the car down
Loose objects make the car lighter
Secured objects make the engine stronger
By Newton's first law, unsecured objects keep moving forward when the car stops suddenly.
What does electronic stability control do?
It helps prevent skidding by braking individual wheels
It inflates the air bags as soon as the car starts
It locks all the doors once the car is moving
It turns on the headlights when it gets dark outside
Stability control senses when the car begins to skid and brakes wheels to help keep control.
Why do cars have laminated windshields made of glass layers with plastic in between?
The glass holds together instead of shattering into pieces
The windshield becomes a mirror
The glass gets hotter in the sun
The windshield can bend like rubber
The plastic layer keeps broken glass stuck together, protecting people from sharp pieces.
Why does a heavier truck take longer to stop than a small car at the same speed?
It has more momentum to change
It has less friction on the road
It has smaller brakes
It moves faster at the same speed
More mass at the same speed means more momentum, which takes more force or time to stop.
Why are side-impact beams built into car doors?
To resist crushing when the car is hit from the side
To make the doors open and close faster and easier
To hold the windows up when the doors are closed
To make the car lighter so it can speed up faster
Strong beams in the doors help protect passengers in side collisions.
Why does a seat belt pretensioner tighten the belt at the start of a crash?
To remove slack so the person is held in place sooner
To make the belt easier to unbuckle
To stretch the belt for comfort
To warn the driver with a sound
Removing slack lets the belt start slowing the person right away.
In a crash, why is it safer to be slowed by an air bag than by the steering wheel?
The air bag slows the person over a longer time and area
The air bag is harder than the wheel
The steering wheel moves away from the driver
The air bag makes the car stop sooner
Spreading the force over more time and a larger area reduces injury.
Why does driving slower in bad weather improve safety?
It reduces stopping distance and crash energy
It increases the car's momentum
It makes air bags inflate faster
It makes the road less slippery
Lower speed means less momentum and kinetic energy, so the car can stop sooner and crashes are less severe.
sciCondIns: Which of these is an electrical conductor?

Which of these is an electrical insulator?

Which of these is an electrical conductor?

Which of these is an electrical insulator?

Which of these is an electrical insulator?
Dry leather does not let electricity flow easily.
Which of these is an electrical conductor?

Why are electrical wires covered in plastic?
Plastic is an insulator that keeps current in the wire
Plastic helps the current flow faster
Plastic is a conductor that adds power

Why are the inside parts of wires usually made of copper?
Copper does not let charge flow

Rubber is an insulator that helps protect them from shocks

A bulb lights when a steel paper clip completes a circuit. What does this show about steel?

Why do the handles of many electrical tools have plastic or rubber grips?

Why is it dangerous to use electrical devices with wet hands?
Water with dissolved salts can conduct electricity
Water turns electricity into heat only

Which material is used in a circuit to let electricity flow from a battery to a bulb?
Metal wires are conductors that carry current around a circuit.
Which of these is an electrical insulator?

Which of these is an electrical conductor?

Why are power lines held on poles by glass or ceramic pieces?

What makes a material a good electrical conductor?

It stops electric charge from moving

In "Velociraptor," what does the name mean?
In Latin, velox means swift and raptor means thief or plunderer.

"Lepidoptera," the order of butterflies and moths, means…

sciXsSciUse: Which two organisms are most closely related?

Which scientific name is written correctly?
The genus is capitalized, the species is lowercase, and the whole name is italicized.

It shares the genus name Canis, the first word of the name.
Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) share the same…

Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
Kingdom, class, phylum, family, order, genus, species

the very same species of bear
types of wild dog in one genus

Who developed the two-name system for naming species?
Linnaeus, a Swedish scientist, popularized binomial nomenclature in the 1700s.
What is the system of giving each species a two-part name called?

When handwriting a scientific name, what can be used in place of italics?

Homo erectus shares the genus Homo, while the others are apes in other genera.
What can you conclude about Lynx canadensis and Lynx rufus?
They are different species in one genus
They are the same species in one genus
They are in two different kingdoms

Which word of a scientific name always starts with a lowercase letter?

Which organism is most closely related to Vulpes vulpes (red fox)?

Why are scientific names useful for classifying organisms?

They tell exactly how big it grows
They list everything the animal eats
They give each animal's age and colour

Which level of classification comes just below kingdom?
Each kingdom is divided into phyla, which are then divided into classes.
sciXsVertEv: Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has moist skin, lays eggs in water, and its young breathe with gills
Amphibians have moist skin and start life in water, breathing with gills.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has dry, scaly skin and lays leathery eggs on land
Reptiles have dry scales and lay eggs with leathery shells on land.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has hollow bones, a beak and feathers
Feathers are found only in birds, which also have beaks and light, hollow bones.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has scales and a lateral line to sense movement in water
A lateral line is a sense organ that fish use to detect movement in the water.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has hair, sweat glands and is warm-blooded
Hair and sweat glands are features found only in mammals.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Starts life as a tadpole and later grows legs and lungs
Amphibians go through metamorphosis from a water-living tadpole to an air-breathing adult.
Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Is cold-blooded, has dry scales and breathes with lungs from birth

Which group does an animal with these traits belong to? Has a backbone, outer ears and hair

Feathers are evidence that the penguin is a bird, even though it swims.
A bat flies, but it has fur and gives birth to live young that drink milk. Which group does it belong to?
Fur and feeding young milk show that bats are mammals.
A salamander has smooth, moist skin and lays its eggs in ponds. Which group does it belong to?
Moist skin without scales and eggs laid in water are evidence of an amphibian.
A turtle has a shell, scaly skin, and lays eggs on land. Which group does it belong to?
Scaly skin and shelled eggs laid on land show a turtle is a reptile.
A shark has gills, fins and a skeleton made of cartilage. Which group does it belong to?
Sharks breathe with gills and swim with fins, so they are fish.
Which piece of evidence best shows that an animal is a bird?
Only birds have feathers; some other animals also lay eggs, fly or walk on two legs.
Which piece of evidence best shows that an animal is a mammal?
Only mammals produce milk to feed their young.
Which evidence best shows an animal is an amphibian rather than a reptile?

It has a backbone and four legs
It is cold-blooded like a reptile
It lays eggs instead of live young
Reptiles have dry, scaly skin, while amphibians have moist, scaleless skin.

It has fins and a strong tail for swimming
It lives in the salt water of the oceans

Breathing with lungs and feeding young milk are traits of mammals, not fish.

Both reptiles and birds lay shelled eggs on land.
Which two groups of vertebrates are warm-blooded?
Birds and mammals keep a steady body temperature, while the other groups are cold-blooded.
A snake has no legs. Which evidence shows it is a reptile, not an amphibian?

Its skin is moist and smooth
It has a long, thin body

Its young hatch in water and breathe with gills
It has four legs and a backbone
It eats insects and other small animals
It is cold-blooded and lays eggs

sciXsAnEv: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?

Which of these animals is a vertebrate?

A sound wave
A beam of light

The stump is always cut open and bleeding
X-rays show the missing limb growing back
Blood tests find a germ that causes the pain
Scans show the brain area for the missing limb is active when phantom pain is felt.
When you touch a hot stove, which cells carry the signal to your spinal cord?
Sensory neurons
Motor neurons
Red blood cells
Muscle fibres
Sensory neurons carry the heat and pain signal from your skin to the spinal cord.
sciXsBehav: Claim: Male fiddler crabs that wave their large claw more often attract more mates. Which evidence supports it?
Females visited males that waved more often
Fiddler crabs live on muddy beaches
Males have one claw much bigger than the other
Fiddler crabs dig burrows in the sand
It directly links more waving to more visits from females, which supports the claim.
Claim: Wolves that hunt in packs raise more pups than lone wolves. Which evidence supports it?
Pack parents raised more pups each year than lone wolves
Wolves howl to keep in touch with the pack
Wolf pups are born in dens in the spring
Grey wolves live in many parts of Canada
It compares the number of pups raised by pack wolves and lone wolves.
Claim: Male frogs with deeper calls attract more mates. Which evidence supports it?
Females moved toward speakers playing deeper calls
Frogs call mostly at night in the spring
Female frogs lay their eggs in ponds
Male frogs have a sac that fills with air
Females choosing deeper calls in an experiment supports the claim.
Claim: Emperor penguin fathers that huddle together in winter hatch more chicks. Which evidence supports it?
Huddling males lost less weight and hatched more eggs
Emperor penguins breed on the ice of Antarctica
Penguins are birds that swim but cannot fly
Penguin fathers keep the egg on their feet
It links huddling to saving energy and to more eggs hatching.
Claim: Salmon that return to the stream where they hatched have more surviving young. Which evidence supports it?
Eggs in home streams survived better than elsewhere
Salmon swim far upstream to lay their eggs
Salmon live in both fresh and salt water
Bears catch many salmon in rivers in the fall
It compares survival of young in home streams with other streams.
Claim: Sea turtles that bury their eggs deeper have more hatchlings. Which evidence supports it?
Deeper nests lost fewer eggs to heat and predators
Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches
Hatchlings crawl to the ocean after hatching
Sea turtles can live for many decades
Fewer lost eggs in deeper nests means more hatchlings, which supports the claim.
Claim: Honeybee colonies whose dances can be followed raise more young. Which evidence supports it?
Hives with readable dances gathered more food for larvae
Honeybees live together in large colonies
Worker bees visit many kinds of flowers
Honeybees make honey from flower nectar
More food gathered from dance information helps the hive raise more young.
Claim: Male sticklebacks that fan their nests have more eggs hatch. Which evidence supports it?
Eggs in fanned nests got more oxygen and more hatched
Sticklebacks are small fish with spines
Male sticklebacks build nests from plants
Stickleback males turn red in the spring
It shows fanning leads to more eggs hatching.
Claim: Caribou calves born at the peak of the calving season survive better. Which evidence supports it?
Calves born at the peak were caught by wolves less often
Caribou travel long distances each year
Caribou calves can walk soon after birth
Caribou eat lichens during the winter
Lower predation on peak-season calves supports the claim.
Claim: Male sage grouse that display in the centre of the lek mate more. Which evidence supports it?
Most matings went to males displaying in the centre
Sage grouse puff out their chest feathers
A lek is an open area where males gather
Sage grouse live in dry grasslands
Observed matings show that central males had more success.
Claim: Birds that mob predators together protect their nests better. Which evidence supports it?
Nests in mobbing colonies lost fewer chicks to crows
Crows are clever birds that eat many foods
Mobbing birds make loud calls and dive
Many birds nest together in colonies
Fewer chicks lost in colonies that mob predators supports the claim.
Claim: Ground squirrels that give alarm calls help their relatives survive and reproduce. Which evidence supports it?
Relatives near callers were caught by predators less often
Ground squirrels live in underground burrows
Alarm calls are short, loud, high sounds
Hawks and badgers hunt ground squirrels
Better survival of relatives near callers supports the claim.
Claim: Beavers that build lodges with underwater entrances raise more kits. Which evidence supports it?
Kits in those lodges were taken by predators less often
Beavers build their lodges from sticks and mud
Beavers have large, orange front teeth
Beavers slap their tails on the water as a warning
Fewer kits lost to predators means more kits raised.
Claim: Female wolf spiders that carry their egg sacs have more spiderlings survive. Which evidence supports it?
More spiderlings hatched from carried sacs than from left sacs
Wolf spiders hunt instead of spinning webs
Spiders have eight legs and no antennae
Spiderlings ride on their mother's back
It compares survival between carried and abandoned egg sacs.
Claim: Male common terns that bring fish to females attract more mates. Which evidence supports it?
Females paired more often with males that brought fish
Terns dive into the water to catch fish
Common terns nest on islands and beaches
Terns migrate long distances each year
Females choosing males that bring food gifts supports the claim.
Claim: Male crickets that chirp more often attract more females. Which evidence supports it?
In tests, females walked toward faster chirping more often
Crickets chirp by rubbing their wings
Crickets are most active on warm nights
Crickets have long antennae and legs
Females choosing faster chirping in tests supports the claim.
Claim: Red squirrels that store more food in the fall have more young in spring. Which evidence supports it?
Squirrels with larger food stores had larger litters
Red squirrels live in conifer forests
Squirrels bury cones and seeds in piles
Red squirrels chatter loudly at intruders
It links bigger food stores to more young.
Claim: Polar bear mothers that stay longer in their dens raise more cubs. Which evidence supports it?
Cubs that left dens later survived more often
Polar bears dig their dens in deep snow drifts
Polar bear cubs are born in the middle of winter
Polar bears hunt seals out on the sea ice
Higher survival for cubs that stayed in dens longer supports the claim.
Claim: Cuckoos whose eggs look like their host's eggs have more chicks survive. Which evidence supports it?
Matching cuckoo eggs were pushed out of nests less often
Cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests
Cuckoo chicks are often larger than hosts
Cuckoos are found in many parts of the world
If hosts reject matching eggs less, more cuckoo chicks survive.
Which evidence would not support the claim that male deer with larger antlers mate more?
Deer antlers fall off each winter and regrow
Males with larger antlers won more fights
Females mated more with large-antlered males
Large-antlered males fathered more fawns
Antlers regrowing says nothing about mating success, while the others link antlers to mating.
Which evidence would weaken the claim that male songbirds that sing at dawn attract more mates?
Males that sang at dawn mated no more than silent males
Males that sang at dawn mated more than silent males
Females flew toward speakers playing dawn songs
Dawn singers fathered more chicks in the study
If dawn singers have no more mates, the evidence does not support the claim.
What makes evidence strong support for a claim about a behaviour and reproduction?
It compares the young raised with and without the behaviour
It describes what colour the animals are
It lists the places where the animals live
It tells how long the animals live in zoos
Comparing offspring for animals with and without the behaviour tests the claim directly.
sciNatSel: Which is the best definition of an adaptation?
An inherited trait that helps survival
A habit learned from a parent
A change made by an injury
A trait that never varies
An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to pass on their genes?
Those best suited to their environment
Those that are the largest in size
Those that live alone the longest
Those that eat the most food
Individuals best suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so their genes are passed on more often.
Darwin studied finches and tortoises on which group of islands?
The Galápagos Islands
The Hawaiian Islands
The Canary Islands
The Magdalen Islands
Darwin's observations on the Galápagos Islands helped him develop the idea of natural selection.
Which of these traits could be passed on by natural selection?
Fur colour
A scar from a fight
A trick learned at a zoo
A tail lost to a predator
Fur colour is controlled by genes, so it can be inherited, unlike injuries or learned behaviours.
Why do most populations produce more offspring than can survive?
Food and space are limited
Parents always abandon their young
Offspring never need any food
Only one offspring is ever born
Because resources are limited, not all offspring survive, so individuals compete and the best-suited ones tend to survive.
What does the phrase "survival of the fittest" mean in biology?
The best-suited organisms reproduce most
The strongest animals win every fight
The fastest runners live the longest
The biggest animals eat the most
In biology, "fit" means well suited to the environment, which leads to more surviving offspring.
A population of beetles includes green and brown beetles. Birds easily spot the green ones on brown soil. Over time, the population will become …
mostly brown
mostly green
half green, half brown
completely white
Brown beetles are better hidden, so more of them survive and reproduce, passing on brown colour.
Natural selection acts on individuals, but which one actually changes over many generations?
The population
A single individual
The weather
The predator's diet
Individuals cannot change their genes; instead the mix of traits in the population changes over generations.
What is the main source of new variation in a population?
Mutations in genes
Exercise during life
Learning from parents
Injuries from predators
Mutations create new versions of genes, which add new inherited variation to a population.
Cacti have thick, waxy stems that store water. This adaptation helps them survive in …
dry deserts
wet rainforests
freshwater ponds
snowy tundra
Storing water and reducing water loss helps cacti survive where rain is rare.
Which of these is a change in a population caused by natural selection?
More hares with thick fur after cold winters
A hare grows thick fur after moving north
A hare learns to hide under a bush
A hare loses fur after a skin injury
Natural selection changes how common an inherited trait is in a population over generations.
Snowshoe hares turn white in winter. How does this help them survive?
It hides them from predators in snow
It keeps them cooler in summer heat
It helps them find more food to eat
It makes them run much faster
White winter fur camouflages hares against snow, so predators such as lynx spot them less often.
A trait that helps an organism survive in one environment might be harmful in …
a different environment
every environment
its own environment
no environment at all
Whether a trait is helpful depends on the environment, so a trait can be useful in one place and harmful in another.
Why can't natural selection make a population change in a single generation?
Trait frequencies shift slowly over generations
Animals refuse to change their habits
Genes change only when organisms grow up
Each individual must decide to adapt
Natural selection works as helpful traits become more common, which takes many generations of reproduction.
Which scientist came up with the idea of natural selection at about the same time as Darwin?
Alfred Russel Wallace
Isaac Newton
Marie Curie
Gregor Mendel
Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea of natural selection, and he and Darwin presented their ideas together in 1858.
What is the term for an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment?
Fitness
Strength
Intelligence
Speed
In biology, fitness describes how well an organism survives and reproduces compared with others.
Which helps a polar bear survive in the Arctic?
Thick fat and dense fur
Thin skin and short fur
Bright colours and spots
Large ears that lose heat
Thick fat and dense fur keep polar bears warm in very cold conditions.
Some weeds now survive a herbicide that used to kill them. What is the best explanation?
Resistant weeds survived and reproduced
The weeds learned to avoid the spray
The herbicide made the weeds stronger
Each weed chose to become resistant
A few weeds had inherited resistance, survived the spray and passed this trait to their offspring.
Which is NOT needed for natural selection to happen?
Organisms trying to change
Variation among individuals
Traits that can be inherited
More offspring than can survive
Natural selection needs variation, inheritance and competition, but not any effort by organisms to change.
Fish in a dark cave over many generations lose working eyes. Which factor most likely allowed this?
Eyes gave no survival advantage there
Fish chose to stop using their eyes
Darkness directly erased their eyes
Predators removed the fish's eyes
In total darkness, eyes do not help survival, so fish without working eyes were not at a disadvantage.
Which word describes features that help an organism blend in with its surroundings?
Camouflage
Mimicry of sound
Migration
Hibernation
Camouflage lets an organism blend in, helping it avoid predators or sneak up on prey.
What evidence did Darwin use to support natural selection?
Variation he saw among living species
Photos of DNA from his microscope
Results from modern gene testing
Satellite images of the islands
Darwin based his ideas on careful observations of variation in living organisms and fossils, long before DNA was understood.
sciXsNatSel: Peppered moths on soot-covered trees: which moths were eaten more often by birds?
Light-coloured moths, which stood out
Dark-coloured moths, which stood out
Both colours were eaten equally
Neither colour was ever eaten
Light moths were easy to see on dark bark, so birds ate them more and dark moths became more common.
After pollution laws cleaned the trees, light peppered moths became common again. Why?
Light moths were hidden on clean bark again
Dark moths all learned to change colour
The cleaner air painted the moths white
Birds stopped eating moths completely
On clean, light bark the light moths were better camouflaged, so they survived and reproduced more.
During a drought, finches with larger, stronger beaks survived better. What is the most likely reason?
They could crack the hard seeds left
They could fly farther to find rain
Their beaks stored extra water
They could sing louder for mates
During the drought only hard seeds remained, so finches with strong beaks got more food and survived.
After the drought, what happened to the average beak size of the next generation of finches?
It became larger
It became smaller
It stayed exactly the same
It disappeared completely
The surviving large-beaked finches passed on their genes, so their offspring had larger beaks on average.
Which explanation of the giraffe's long neck matches natural selection?
Longer-necked giraffes survived and had more young
Giraffes stretched their necks and passed it on
Giraffes grew long necks because they wanted to
Each giraffe's neck grew after eating leaves
Natural selection explains change through inherited variation and differences in survival, not by stretching or wanting.
Why is the idea that giraffes stretched their necks and passed this on incorrect?
Changes made during life are not inherited
Giraffes cannot stretch their necks at all
Necks are not used to reach food
Giraffes never have any offspring
Body changes gained during a lifetime do not change genes, so they cannot be passed to offspring.
A new predator that hunts by sight arrives on an island with green and red lizards living on green plants. Which prediction best follows natural selection?
Green lizards will become more common
Red lizards will become more common
All lizards will turn blue
The number of each colour stays equal
Green lizards are camouflaged against green plants, so fewer are caught and more of them reproduce.
Some mosquitoes in an area survive a common insecticide. What explains this best?
Some already had genes for resistance
The insecticide gave them resistance
They avoided the spray by choice
They grew resistant after being sprayed
A few mosquitoes already had resistance genes; they survived the spray and passed these genes on.
Why do doctors tell patients to finish all of their antibiotics?
To avoid leaving resistant bacteria alive
To make the bacteria grow faster
To help the bacteria become stronger
To make the medicine taste better
Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive, and they may multiply into a resistant population.
Rock pocket mice live on light sand and on dark lava rock. Which pattern would natural selection produce?
Dark mice on lava, light mice on sand
Light mice on lava, dark mice on sand
Only light mice in both places
Only dark mice in both places
In each habitat the mice that match their background are hidden from predators, so they survive and reproduce more.
A population of identical bacterial clones is exposed to an antibiotic, and none are resistant. What is most likely?
No resistance develops; they all die
All of them quickly become resistant
Half of them become resistant at once
They all learn to avoid the drug
Without variation there is no resistant individual to be selected, so resistance cannot spread.
Which observation shows that a trait is inherited?
Offspring share the trait with parents
The trait appears only after injury
The trait is learned in a classroom
The trait changes with each meal
When offspring share a trait with their parents, it is passed on through genes and can be acted on by natural selection.
Two populations of the same bird species live in different habitats for thousands of years. What might eventually happen?
They may become separate species
They will become identical copies
They will both stop reproducing
They will all migrate together
Different environments favour different traits, so isolated populations can change until they become separate species.
Arctic foxes have small ears and short legs. How does natural selection explain this?
Foxes that lost less heat survived better
Foxes shrank their ears to stay warm
Cold weather made each fox's ears smaller
Foxes chose shorter legs for snow
Small ears and short legs reduce heat loss, so foxes with these inherited traits survived and reproduced more in the cold.
Hunters often target elephants with large tusks. Over many years, what has happened in some populations?
More elephants are born without tusks
Elephants grow larger tusks than before
Elephants learn to hide their tusks
Tusk size stays exactly the same
Tuskless elephants were less likely to be hunted, so they survived and passed on this trait more often.
A fish population in a stream has both fast and slow swimmers. A fast predator is introduced. Predict what happens.
Fast swimmers become more common
Slow swimmers become more common
All fish become slow swimmers
The fish stop swimming entirely
Fast swimmers escape the predator more often, so they live to reproduce and pass on this trait.
Which statement correctly uses the idea of natural selection?
Helpful traits become common over generations
Animals change on purpose to fit in
All individuals in a group are identical
Traits change in a single lifetime
Natural selection makes helpful inherited traits more common in a population over many generations.
A disease kills most rabbits, but a few survive because of a gene. What happens to later generations?
More rabbits carry the protective gene
Fewer rabbits carry the protective gene
All rabbits lose the protective gene
No rabbit is ever born again
Survivors pass the protective gene to their offspring, so it becomes more common in the population.
Why do different species of Darwin's finches have different beak shapes on different islands?
Each island favoured beaks fit for its foods
Finches reshaped their beaks by pecking
Each finch picked a beak it liked
The islands all had identical foods
Different food sources on each island favoured different beak shapes, leading to different finch species.
Which piece of evidence would best support that natural selection changed a population?
Trait records over many generations
One photo of a single animal
A story about one animal's habits
The colour of one leaf in spring
Data on how common a trait is across many generations shows whether a population has changed.
Why is reproduction important for natural selection to change a population?
Traits pass on only through offspring
Reproduction makes animals stronger
Offspring choose their own traits
Reproduction stops all variation
Only traits passed to offspring can become more common, so survival alone is not enough without reproduction.
Walking-stick insects look like twigs. Which explanation is best?
Twig-like insects were eaten less often
Insects copied twigs by practising
Twigs turned some insects into sticks
Birds taught the insects to look odd
Insects that looked more like twigs were missed by predators, so they survived and passed on their shape.
sciXsFlCon: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
The anther, at the top of the stamen, produces pollen grains.
Which part of a flower catches pollen?
The sticky stigma at the top of the pistil traps pollen during pollination.
After fertilization, what does a flower's ovary develop into?
The ovary swells and ripens into the fruit, which surrounds and protects the seeds.
What does an ovule become after fertilization?
Each fertilized ovule develops into a seed containing a tiny plant.
Why do many flowers have bright petals and sweet nectar?
Colour and nectar attract insects and birds that carry pollen from flower to flower.
Conifer seeds are often described as "naked." What does this mean?
They are not enclosed in a fruit
They have no outer seed coat
Conifers are gymnosperms, meaning their seeds sit exposed on cone scales rather than inside a fruit.
Which of these plants is a conifer?
White spruce produces cones and needle-like leaves, so it is a conifer.
What is the first step in the life cycle of a seed plant once a seed lands in good soil?
Germination is when the seed sprouts and the young plant begins to grow.
What must happen before a flower can produce seeds?
The stem must lose its leaves
Pollination brings pollen to the stigma, which allows fertilization and seed development.
Male and female pine cones differ. Which describes male cones?
Male cones are small and soft and release large amounts of pollen into the wind.
Why do conifers produce huge amounts of pollen?
Wind pollination is a matter of chance
Insects need extra food to eat
Wind carries pollen randomly, so making lots of it increases the chance some reaches a female cone.
How do burrs, like burdock, spread their seeds?
By being blown by wind wings
Burrs have tiny hooks that catch on fur or clothing and are carried away.
Each dandelion seed has a fluffy parachute that lets the wind carry it far away.
How do animals help spread the seeds of fruits like blueberries?
They eat the fruit and drop the seeds
They plant the seeds on purpose
They carry pollen to the cones
They bury the leaves in soil
Animals eat the fruit and later pass the seeds in their droppings, often far from the parent plant.
Which is a key difference between flowering plants and conifers?
Both make seeds, but only flowering plants enclose their seeds in fruit.
Jack pine cones often stay closed until a certain event opens them. What is it?
The heat of a forest fire
Jack pine cones are sealed with resin that melts in the heat of a fire, releasing the seeds.
What is the young plant inside a seed called?
The embryo is the tiny undeveloped plant inside a seed.
What is the job of a seed's stored food?
To feed the young plant as it sprouts
To attract pollinators to the seed
To make the seed heavier for wind
To help the seed make pollen
The stored food gives the embryo energy until it can make its own food by photosynthesis.
Which is the correct order in the life cycle of a flowering plant?
A seed grows into a seedling, which matures and flowers, then forms fruit containing new seeds.
Which is the correct order in the life cycle of a pine tree?
A pine seed grows into a seedling and then a mature tree, which produces cones that hold new seeds.
What happens to a flower's petals after pollination and fertilization?
They usually wilt and fall off
Once fertilized, the flower no longer needs to attract pollinators, so the petals often wither while the fruit develops.
Maple trees produce winged seeds called samaras. How do these seeds travel?
Samaras have wings that make them spin like helicopters, letting the wind carry them away from the tree.
sciXsMossFern: Which is true about mosses?
They have no true roots, stems or leaves
They grow taller than most trees
They produce seeds inside fruit
They make pollen in small cones
Mosses are non-vascular plants that lack true roots, stems and leaves.
What tiny root-like threads hold a moss in place?
Rhizoids
Fronds
Cones
Petals
Rhizoids anchor mosses to soil or rock but do not carry water like real roots.
How do mosses take in water?
Directly through their surfaces
Through deep woody roots
Through tubes in a thick trunk
Through flowers and fruit
Lacking vascular tissue, mosses absorb water directly through their thin leaf-like parts.
What is the large leaf of a fern called?
A frond
A needle
A capsule
A petal
A fern's leaves are called fronds, and they often unroll from fiddleheads.
Where does a fern's underground stem grow?
Below the soil as a rhizome
High in the air as a trunk
Inside the spore capsule
On the tips of its fronds
Most ferns have an underground stem called a rhizome from which fronds and roots grow.
Which of these plants reproduces with spores, not seeds?
Sphagnum moss
Sugar maple
White pine
Wild rose
Sphagnum is a moss, and mosses reproduce with spores rather than seeds.
How is a spore different from a seed?
A spore has no stored food or embryo
A spore is much larger than a seed
A spore grows only inside fruit
A spore is made only in cones
A spore is a single cell without an embryo or food supply, while a seed contains both.
Ferns and mosses have two stages in their life cycle. What is this called?
Alternation of generations
Complete metamorphosis
Seed dispersal
Cross-pollination
Their life cycle switches between a spore-making stage and a sex-cell-making stage, called alternation of generations.
In a fern, which stage is the large, leafy plant we usually see?
The spore-producing stage
The heart-shaped stage
The egg-producing stage
The seed-producing stage
The familiar leafy fern is the sporophyte, the stage that makes spores.
In a moss, which stage is the green, leafy carpet we usually see?
The egg- and sperm-producing stage
The seed-producing stage
The pollen-producing stage
The fruit-producing stage
The green moss plant is the gametophyte, which makes eggs and sperm.
What grows from a fertilized egg on a fern prothallus?
A new leafy fern plant
A new spore capsule
A flower and fruit
A pine cone
The fertilized egg develops into the young leafy fern, which grows out of the prothallus.
What grows from a fertilized egg on a moss plant?
A stalk with a spore capsule
A new set of fronds
A small woody tree
A flower with petals
In mosses, the fertilized egg grows into a stalk topped with a capsule that makes spores.
What does a moss spore grow into when it lands in a damp spot?
A new green moss plant
A tall fern frond
A seed with a coat
A heart-shaped cone
A moss spore germinates into a thread-like growth that develops into a new green moss plant.
Why are mosses often called pioneer plants?
They can grow on bare rock first
They only grow in pine forests
They grow after all other plants
They need deep, rich soil
Mosses can colonize bare rock and help build soil that other plants later use.
Why can ferns grow taller than mosses?
Their vascular tissue moves water upward
They take in water through their spores
They have no need for any water
They store water in their fiddleheads
Vascular tissue carries water and nutrients up the plant, letting ferns grow larger.
What do the brown dots under a fern frond contain?
Spore cases full of spores
Seeds wrapped in fruit
Pollen for the wind
Stored drops of water
The brown dots are sori, clusters of spore cases that release spores.
How are fern spores released?
Spore cases dry and burst open
Bees carry them from flowers
Animals eat and drop them
They fall from ripe cones
When spore cases dry out they split open and fling spores into the air.
Which group of plants includes both mosses and ferns?
Seedless plants
Flowering plants
Conifers
Fruit trees
Mosses and ferns are seedless plants because they reproduce by spores.
Which habitat best suits most mosses?
A shady, damp forest floor
A dry, sunny desert dune
A salty, windy beach
A hot, rocky volcano top
Mosses need moisture for water uptake and for sperm to swim, so damp, shady places suit them.
A fern prothallus makes which of the following?
Eggs and sperm
Seeds and fruit
Pollen and cones
Flowers and nectar
The small heart-shaped prothallus produces eggs and sperm for sexual reproduction.
Fiddleheads of the ostrich fern are eaten in New Brunswick. What part of the fern are they?
Young fronds that are tightly curled
Seeds that grow inside fruit
Roots that grow below the soil
Spore cases that hang from stems
Fiddleheads are young, coiled fronds that unroll as the fern grows.
Peat moss is used by gardeners. Which property makes it useful in soil?
It holds a lot of water
It makes soil very dry
It adds sharp sand to soil
It produces many new seeds
Sphagnum peat moss soaks up and holds water, helping keep soil moist.
sciPhotoE: What liquid do plants take in through their roots for photosynthesis?
Plants absorb water through their roots and use it in photosynthesis.
Plants use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Through which tiny openings do leaves take in carbon dioxide?
Stomata are small pores, mostly on the underside of leaves, that let gases in and out.
Which part of most plants does the most photosynthesis?
Leaves are broad and full of chloroplasts, so they capture the most light.
Where is the energy from sunlight stored after photosynthesis?
Light energy is changed into chemical energy stored in glucose molecules.
How do plants release the energy stored in glucose?
Cellular respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to release usable energy.
Which process happens in plant cells both day and night?
Photosynthesis needs light, but cells respire all the time to get energy.
What do plants use some of their glucose to build?
Plants link glucose into cellulose, which forms strong cell walls.
How do plants store extra glucose for later?
Plants join glucose molecules into starch, which they store in roots, seeds and stems.
Leaves are full of green water
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green.
What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when a plant is moved into darkness?
Photosynthesis needs light energy, so without light it cannot happen.
Which energy change happens when an animal eats a plant?
Chemical energy passes to the animal
Light energy passes to the animal
Sound energy passes to the animal
Nuclear energy passes to the animal
The chemical energy stored in the plant's food is transferred to the animal that eats it.
Plants produce their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers.
Where did the oxygen in the air we breathe mostly come from?
Photosynthesis by plants, algae and cyanobacteria released most of Earth's atmospheric oxygen.
Which tissue carries water from roots up to the leaves?
Xylem tubes carry water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.
Which tissue carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant?
Phloem tubes move sugars from the leaves to roots, stems, fruits and seeds.
A student puts a pondweed under a bright lamp and sees bubbles. What gas is in the bubbles?
Pondweed releases oxygen during photosynthesis, which forms bubbles in the water.
If the lamp is moved closer to the pondweed, what most likely happens to the bubbles?
More light increases the rate of photosynthesis, so more oxygen bubbles are released.
Why do maple leaves turn red and yellow in fall?
Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing other pigments
Leaves fill up with extra chlorophyll
Cold air paints the leaves new colours

Which organisms depend on photosynthesis for their food energy?

Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?

Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?

Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?

Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?

Which of these organisms carries out photosynthesis?

sciPopEco: Which level of organization is this? All the beavers living along one river.

One individual living thing is an organism, the simplest of these levels.

Many different species living together in an area make a community.
sciORG: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?

Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light.

Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria to release energy from food.
What is the main job of the nucleus?

To give the cell a stiff shape
The nucleus holds the cell's DNA and directs the cell's activities.
What does a cell's DNA contain?
DNA carries the genetic instructions that tell the cell how to grow and work.

Which structure inside the nucleus helps make ribosomes?

Why do muscle cells contain many mitochondria?

Why do leaf cells have more chloroplasts than root cells?

Which organelle is like a factory's manager's office, holding the plans?

Which organelle is like a storage warehouse?
Vacuoles store water, food and wastes, much like a warehouse stores supplies.

Sea anemones

Too much salt washing off land

A zone where boats can dump waste

A cold, deep hiding spot
A source of fresh water

Water made deep inside rocks

Pavement

None of it
All of it
A thin sliver

Which is the best model for showing why we see Moon phases?

A map of Canada's provinces
A globe without any light source
A drawing of the planets' sizes

Summer
Spring
Autumn

The umbra
The corona
The eclipse

During a partial lunar eclipse, what do we see?
Part of the Moon in Earth's dark shadow
The whole Moon turning bright blue
The Sun completely covered by the Moon
The Moon vanishing from the sky
