The Moon turns completely black
The Moon blocks the Sun's light
The Moon moves closer to Earth

Blue moon
Harvest moon
New moon

The Moon's shadow falls on Earth
The Sun's shadow falls on Earth
Mars's shadow falls on the Moon

It happens only in the daytime
It can be seen only at the poles
It lasts for only a few seconds

Why is it safe to look at a lunar eclipse?

Completely outside the shadow
Between Earth and the Sun
Only touching the penumbra

Earth is round
Earth is flat
The Moon is square
The Sun is shrinking

More sunlight reaching the Moon
The Moon moving closer to the Sun
Fewer clouds anywhere on Earth

The Sun turns red every evening

A few seconds
Several weeks

They can only happen at new moon

They happen only during the day

The Moon makes some of its own light
Streetlights shine onto the Moon
Stars light up the Moon's surface
Earth's atmosphere refracts some sunlight into the shadow, dimly lighting the Moon.

Earth's umbra
The Moon
They are exactly equal
Neither exists

Partial, total, then penumbral
Total, penumbral, then partial

What would an astronaut standing on the Moon see during a lunar eclipse?
Earth blocking the Sun
The Moon blocking Earth
The Sun blocking Earth
Mars blocking the Sun

What tool do you need to watch a lunar eclipse?
Just your eyes
Special eclipse glasses
A welding mask
A pinhole projector

A lunar eclipse happens at 2 a.m. in Ontario. Who on Earth could see it?
People where it is night
Only people in Ontario
Only people at the equator
People where it is daytime

Why eclipses do not happen monthly
Why the Moon shines at night
Why Earth has four seasons
Why the Moon is grey

During a lunar eclipse, Earth is located …
between the Sun and the Moon
behind the Moon
beside the Sun
far from the Moon's orbit

What is the main difference between the umbra and the penumbra?
The umbra blocks all direct sunlight
The penumbra blocks all direct sunlight
The umbra is lighter in colour
The penumbra is the inner shadow
In the umbra, Earth blocks all direct sunlight; in the penumbra, only part of it.
sciXsUniv: A huge ball of hot gas that makes its own light
A rocky body that reflects sunlight
A small icy body with a long tail
A cloud of dust that gives no light

What is the nearest star to Earth?
The Sun is a star and is far closer to Earth than any other star.
After the Sun, what is the nearest known star to Earth?

A star and the objects that orbit it
A group of galaxies held together
A single planet and its moons
A cloud of gas between galaxies

Which list is in order from largest to smallest?
The universe contains galaxies, which contain solar systems, which contain planets.
A group of galaxies held by gravity
A group of planets around a star
A group of moons around a planet
A group of comets near the Sun
Galaxy clusters contain hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound together by gravity.
What is the name of the small group of galaxies that includes the Milky Way?
The Milky Way, Andromeda and dozens of smaller galaxies form the Local Group.
Where is our solar system located in the Milky Way?
In one of the spiral arms
Our solar system lies in a spiral arm, about two thirds of the way out from the centre.

Roughly how many stars are in the Milky Way?
The Milky Way is estimated to contain roughly 100 to 400 billion stars.
Which theory describes how the universe began expanding from a hot, dense state?

About how old is the universe?

Stars all stay in fixed places

Why do astronomers measure distances to stars in light-years instead of kilometres?

The Milky Way galaxy contains our whole solar system and billions of other stars.
The Moon is smaller than Earth, Jupiter and the Sun.
What force keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them in orbit.
What do astronomers call the band of light across the night sky on a dark, clear night?

Burning coal deep in their cores

A group of planets orbiting a star
A type of galaxy with arms
A cloud where stars are born
Constellations are star patterns as seen from Earth; their stars are often at very different distances.

No gas or dust at all

sciPlates: What happens at a divergent boundary?
At divergent boundaries, plates separate and magma rises to fill the gap.
What happens at a convergent boundary?
At convergent boundaries, plates collide, causing subduction or mountain building.
What happens at a transform boundary?
At transform boundaries, plates grind sideways past one another.
Which feature forms where an ocean plate sinks beneath another plate?
Subduction bends the sinking plate downward, creating a deep trench.
Which feature forms where two ocean plates move apart?
Magma rising between separating ocean plates builds an underwater mountain range.
Which type of plate boundary is described? The Juan de Fuca Plate sinks beneath North America off the BC coast.
One plate sinking under another is subduction, which happens at convergent boundaries.
Which type of plate boundary is described? The Queen Charlotte Fault, where plates slide sideways off Haida Gwaii.
Plates sliding horizontally past each other form a transform boundary.
Which type of plate boundary is described? Iceland is slowly being pulled apart along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates move apart.
Which type of plate boundary is described? The Andes Mountains rise where an ocean plate dives under South America.
Subduction of the Nazca Plate under South America builds the Andes.
Which type of plate boundary is described? The Red Sea is slowly widening as Africa and Arabia separate.
The Red Sea is a young ocean forming as plates pull apart.
Which type of plate boundary is described? The Mariana Trench forms where one ocean plate sinks under another.
Ocean-ocean subduction at a convergent boundary formed the Mariana Trench.
Which type of plate boundary is described? New Zealand's Alpine Fault, where plates mostly slide past each other.
The Alpine Fault is mainly a transform boundary with sideways motion.
Which feature is NOT usually formed at a convergent boundary?
Mid-ocean ridges form at divergent boundaries where plates move apart.
At which type of boundary is crust created?
Magma rises and cools between separating plates, forming new crust.
At which type of boundary is crust destroyed as it sinks into the mantle?
At subduction zones, crust sinks into the mantle and is recycled.
What usually happens when two continental plates collide?
The crust crumples into high mountains
A deep trench forms between them
New ocean floor forms between them

Why does an ocean plate sink when it meets a continental plate?
Denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the more buoyant continental crust.
What is thought to drive the movement of tectonic plates?
Heat from Earth's interior causes slow mantle flow that helps move the plates.
Which scientist proposed the idea of continental drift?
In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had once been joined and drifted apart.
Which evidence supports the idea that continents were once joined?

Why are volcanoes common around the Pacific "Ring of Fire"?

The Pacific has no plate boundaries
The Pacific is the warmest ocean

About how fast do tectonic plates move?

sciXsAtomEl: Which particle has a positive charge?

A substance made of only one kind of atom
A mixture that can be separated by hand
A single particle inside the nucleus

Which element has the lightest atoms?

How many atoms in total are in one molecule of C₆H₁₂O₆?

The balls are joined by a stick
It is a gas at room temperature

sciXsRxEnergy: Which describes the energy change? Natural gas burning in a furnace
Combustion gives off heat and light to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Iron slowly rusting on a bike chain
Rusting slowly releases heat as iron combines with oxygen, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Cells breaking down glucose in cellular respiration
Respiration releases energy stored in glucose, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? A candle burning on a table
Burning wax gives off heat and light, so energy is released.
Which describes the energy change? A glow stick giving off light after it is bent
The chemicals react and release energy as light, so the reaction is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? An acid and a base mixing and the beaker getting warm
The beaker warms because the neutralization releases energy.
Which describes the energy change? Wet concrete warming up as it hardens
The setting reaction in concrete releases heat, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Electricity splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen
Electrolysis needs a constant input of electrical energy, so it absorbs energy.
Which describes the energy change? Citric acid and baking soda in water making the cup feel cold
The cup cools because the reaction takes in thermal energy from its surroundings.
Which describes the energy change? Limestone breaking down into lime when heated in a kiln

Ordinary hydrogen has just one proton and one electron, with no neutrons.
An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its atomic number?
The atomic number is the number of protons, which is 11.
Protons repel each other. What holds them together in the nucleus?
The strong nuclear force acts over tiny distances and is stronger than the repulsion between protons.
In a model of an atom, which part is at the very centre?
The nucleus is the small, dense centre of the atom.
sciMIX: Classify neon gas as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Neon is made of only one kind of atom.
Classify aluminum foil as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Aluminum foil is made of aluminum atoms only.
Classify liquid mercury as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Mercury is a pure substance made of one kind of atom.
Classify yellow sulfur powder as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Sulfur is made of only sulfur atoms.
Classify nitrogen gas (N₂) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
N₂ molecules contain only nitrogen atoms.
Classify copper wire as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Copper wire is made of copper atoms only.
Classify baking soda (NaHCO₃) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Baking soda is sodium, hydrogen, carbon and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Classify rust (Fe₂O₃) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Rust is iron and oxygen chemically bonded together.
Classify ammonia (NH₃) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Each ammonia molecule has nitrogen and hydrogen atoms bonded together.
Classify methane (CH₄) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Methane is carbon and hydrogen chemically combined.
Classify glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Glucose is one pure substance made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen bonded together.
Classify calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Calcium carbonate contains three elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Classify trail mix as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
You can see and pick out the separate nuts, raisins and seeds.
Classify granite as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Granite has visible grains of different minerals mixed together.
Classify a slice of pizza as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
The crust, sauce, cheese and toppings are separate parts you can see.
Classify sand mixed with iron filings as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
The two parts stay separate and can be pulled apart with a magnet.
Classify cereal in milk as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
The cereal pieces and milk are visibly different parts.
Classify vinegar as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Vinegar is acetic acid evenly dissolved in water, so it looks like one substance.
Classify brass as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Brass is an alloy in which zinc is evenly mixed into copper.
Classify clear apple juice as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Sugars and other substances are dissolved evenly in water, so you see only one phase.
Classify maple syrup as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
Maple syrup is sugar evenly dissolved in water.
Classify sugar stirred into hot tea until it disappears as an element, a compound, a mechanical mixture or a solution.
The dissolved sugar spreads evenly through the tea and can't be seen.
sciXsAngCon: Which group of plants makes seeds that are not covered by a fruit?
Gymnosperms such as pines carry their seeds exposed on cone scales instead of inside a fruit.
Which structure do angiosperms use for sexual reproduction?
Angiosperms are the flowering plants, and their flowers contain the male and female reproductive parts.
In a conifer, where is pollen made?
Conifers make pollen in small, soft male cones that release it into the wind.
In a pine tree, where do the ovules develop?
At the tips of the roots
Female (seed) cones carry ovules on their scales, which become seeds after fertilization.
How is pollen usually carried from one conifer to another?
Conifers have no flowers to attract animals, so their light pollen is carried by the wind.
Which part of a flower makes pollen?
The anther, at the top of the stamen, produces the pollen grains.
Which part of a flower is sticky and catches pollen?
The stigma at the top of the pistil is sticky so pollen grains attach to it.
After fertilization in a flower, what does an ovule become?
Each fertilized ovule develops into a seed, while the ovary around it becomes the fruit.
What grows down from a pollen grain to reach the ovule?
A pollen tube grows from the pollen grain through the style to carry sperm to the ovule.
Which of these plants is a gymnosperm?
Spruces are conifers that make seeds in cones, so they are gymnosperms.
Which of these plants is an angiosperm?
Oaks produce flowers and acorns (fruits), so they are angiosperms; the others are conifers.
Why do many flowers have bright petals and sweet nectar?
Colour and nectar attract animals such as bees that carry pollen from flower to flower.
What is the main job of a fruit in an angiosperm's life cycle?
Fruits protect the seeds and help them spread, for example when animals eat the fruit.
In the conifer life cycle, about how long can it take a pine cone's seeds to mature after pollination?
In many pines, fertilization happens about a year after pollination and the seeds mature in roughly two years.
Which part of a flower contains the ovules?
The ovary at the base of the pistil holds the ovules, which become seeds.
What is the male part of a flower called?
The stamen, made of the anther and filament, is the male reproductive part.
What is the female part of a flower called?
The pistil, made of stigma, style and ovary, is the female reproductive part.
What is the first stage after a seed lands in good conditions?
Germination is when the seed absorbs water and the young plant starts to grow.
Pollen moving to a female part
Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma (in flowers) or to the ovule (in cones).
How do the seeds of a maple tree spread?
Winged fruits spin in the wind
They stick to fur with hooks
Maple fruits (samaras) have wings that spin and carry seeds away on the wind.
Which statement compares conifers and flowering plants correctly?
Conifers and angiosperms are both seed plants, but only angiosperms enclose seeds in fruit.
Which tissue in a seed feeds the young plant until it can make its own food?
The seed's stored food, such as the endosperm, nourishes the embryo during germination.
sciECR: Which relationship is shown? A mosquito sucks blood from a deer.
The mosquito benefits by feeding while the deer is harmed but not killed.
Which relationship is shown? An owl swoops down and eats a vole.
The owl kills and eats the vole, so one organism hunts another for food.
Which relationship is shown? Oxpecker birds eat ticks off a rhino's skin.
The birds get food and the rhino gets rid of parasites, so both benefit.
Which relationship is shown? A remora rides on a shark and eats scraps of its meals.
The remora gets food and transport while the shark is neither helped nor harmed.
Which relationship is shown? A lynx chases and eats a snowshoe hare.
The lynx is a predator that kills and eats the hare, its prey.
Which relationship is shown? Lice live in a child's hair and feed on blood.
Lice benefit by feeding on the person, who is harmed.
Which relationship is shown? Bacteria in a cow's stomach digest grass and get a home.
The bacteria get food and shelter and the cow can digest grass, so both benefit.
Which relationship is shown? A spider spins its web between a plant's stems.
The spider gets a place to build while the plant is unaffected.
Which relationship is shown? A wolf pack hunts a moose.
The wolves kill and eat the moose for food.
Which relationship is shown? A hummingbird drinks nectar and carries pollen to other flowers.
The bird gets food and the plant gets pollinated, so both benefit.
Which relationship is shown? A leech attaches to a swimmer's leg to feed on blood.
The leech benefits while the swimmer is harmed.
Which relationship is shown? Cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows.
The egrets get an easy meal while the cows are not affected.
Which relationship is shown? A heron spears and eats a fish.
The heron hunts, kills and eats the fish.
Which relationship is shown? Mistletoe grows into a tree and takes its water and nutrients.
The mistletoe benefits by taking resources while the host tree is harmed.
Which relationship is shown? Fungi on tree roots get sugar and help the tree take in water.
The fungus gets food and the tree gets water and minerals, so both benefit.
Which relationship is shown? A hermit crab lives in an empty snail shell.
The crab gets shelter and the snail, already gone, is not affected.
Which relationship is shown? A ladybug eats aphids on a rose bush.
The ladybug kills and eats the aphids as prey.
Which relationship is shown? A cleaner shrimp eats parasites from a fish's mouth.
The shrimp gets food and the fish is cleaned, so both benefit.
Which relationship is shown? A tick burrows into a moose's skin and drinks its blood.
The tick benefits by feeding while the moose is harmed.
Which relationship is shown? A squirrel nests in a hole in a large tree.
The squirrel gets shelter while the tree is not helped or harmed.
Which relationship is shown? A polar bear catches and eats a seal.
The polar bear hunts and eats the seal.
Which relationship is shown? Ants protect an acacia tree, which gives them food and shelter.
The ants get food and homes and the tree is protected, so both benefit.
sciEcoRel: Which relationship is this? Two trees grow close together and both need the same sunlight.
Both trees need the same limited resource, so each is harmed by the other.
Which relationship is this? Wolves and coyotes both hunt the same deer in an area.
Both predators rely on the same limited prey, so they compete.
Which relationship is this? A tapeworm lives inside a dog's gut and absorbs its food.
The tapeworm benefits while the dog loses nutrients and is harmed.
Which relationship is this? A peregrine falcon dives and catches a pigeon.
The falcon kills and eats the pigeon.
Which relationship is this? Lichen is made of a fungus and an alga that help each other.
The alga makes food by photosynthesis and the fungus gives shelter and moisture, so both benefit.
Which relationship is this? Burdock seeds hook onto a fox's fur and are carried away.
The plant's seeds are spread while the fox is basically unaffected.
Which relationship is this? Cowbirds lay eggs in warblers' nests, and the warblers raise the chicks.
The cowbird benefits while the warbler wastes energy raising another bird's young.
Which relationship is this? Bluejays and squirrels both gather the same acorns.
Both animals need the same limited food supply.
Which relationship is this? Root nodule bacteria give a clover plant nitrogen and get sugars.
The bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant and receive food, so both benefit.
Which relationship is this? A great white shark attacks and eats a seal.
The shark is a predator and the seal is its prey.
Which relationship is this? Barn swallows nest under the roof of a barn used by horses.
The swallows gain shelter while the horses are not affected.
Which relationship is this? Dandelions and grass on a lawn take water from the same soil.
Both plants need the same limited water and nutrients.
Which relationship is this? A flea lives on a cat and bites it for blood.
The flea benefits while the cat is harmed.
Which relationship is this? A garter snake swallows a frog.
The snake kills and eats the frog.
Which relationship is this? Humans grow crops for pollinating bees and the bees pollinate the crops.
Bees get nectar and pollen while crops get pollinated, so both benefit.
Which relationship is this? A woodpecker drills a hole in a dead tree for its nest.
The woodpecker benefits, and the dead tree is neither helped nor harmed.
Which relationship is this? Lions and hyenas fight over the same zebra carcass.
Both species want the same limited food, so they compete.
Which relationship is this? A dragonfly catches a mosquito in mid-air.
The dragonfly hunts and eats the mosquito.
Which relationship is this? A sea lamprey attaches to a lake trout and feeds on its blood.
The lamprey benefits while the trout is harmed and may weaken.
Which relationship is this? Clownfish live among sea anemone tentacles and chase off fish that eat anemones.
The clownfish gets protection and the anemone gets defended, so both benefit.
Which relationship is this? Moss grows on the north side of a tree trunk without harming it.
The moss gets a place to grow and the tree is unaffected.
Which relationship is this? Two male deer fight to mate with the same females.
Members of the same species compete for a limited resource, here mates.
sciXsSymb: What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A tapeworm lives in a wolf's intestine and absorbs its food
The tapeworm benefits while the wolf loses nutrients.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Gut bacteria in humans help digest food and get a place to live
Both the bacteria and the human benefit.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? An orchid grows on a rainforest tree to reach sunlight
The orchid benefits and the tree is neither helped nor harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Mistletoe takes water and nutrients from a host tree
The mistletoe benefits while the tree is weakened.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Oxpeckers eat ticks from a zebra's back
The bird gets food and the zebra loses parasites, so both benefit.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A remora attaches to a shark and eats leftover scraps
The remora benefits and the shark is unaffected.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Head lice feed on blood from a person's scalp
The lice benefit while the person is harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A fungus and an alga live together as a lichen
The alga provides food and the fungus provides shelter and moisture.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Spanish moss hangs from tree branches without taking nutrients
The moss gets support and the tree is not harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A mosquito drinks blood from a moose
The mosquito benefits while the moose is harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Ants protect aphids and eat the sweet honeydew they make
The ants get food and the aphids get protection.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A hermit crab uses an empty snail shell as its home
The crab benefits and the snail is not affected.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A cuckoo lays its egg in another bird's nest to be raised
The cuckoo benefits while the host bird wastes effort raising its chick.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Cleaner wrasse fish eat parasites off larger fish
The cleaner gets food and the larger fish gets cleaned.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Cattle egrets eat insects disturbed by grazing cattle
The egret benefits and the cattle are unaffected.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A sea lamprey clings to a fish and feeds on its blood
The lamprey benefits while the fish is harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in pea plant roots and get sugar
The bacteria give the plant nitrogen and receive food, so both benefit.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A bird builds its nest in the branches of a spruce
The bird gets a nest site and the tree is unaffected.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? Heartworms live in a dog's heart and make it sick
The worms benefit while the dog is harmed.
What kind of symbiotic relationship is this? A hummingbird feeds on nectar and pollinates the flower
The bird gets food and the plant gets pollinated.
Which symbiotic relationship helps one organism and does not affect the other?
In commensalism one partner benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.
Which symbiotic relationship helps both organisms?
In mutualism both partners benefit from living together.
sciXsSucc: What are the first organisms to live on bare rock called?
Pioneer species such as lichens are the first to colonize bare, lifeless areas.
What kind of succession happens on a brand-new volcanic island?
Primary succession starts where there is no soil, such as fresh lava rock.
Which is needed before most plants can grow on a new volcanic island?
Most plants need soil to anchor roots and get nutrients, so soil must form first.
What is the stable community at the end of succession called?
A climax community is the fairly stable community that develops last in succession.
Which order is typical for primary succession on lava rock?
Lichens and mosses build soil first, then larger plants can grow as the soil deepens.
How might seeds first reach a new volcanic island?
Carried by wind, waves or birds
Dug up from under the rock
Seeds and spores arrive from elsewhere on the wind, on floating material or with birds.
Why can mosses grow after lichens on volcanic rock?
Lichens left a thin layer of soil
Lichens turned the rock to sand
Lichens break down rock and add organic matter, creating a thin soil where mosses can grow.
Which event leads to secondary succession, not primary?
A forest fire that leaves soil
A new island rising from sea
After a fire the soil remains, so regrowth is secondary succession.
Which event can start primary succession?
A glacier retreating from bare rock
A retreating glacier leaves bare rock with no soil, where primary succession begins.
Why is primary succession usually slower than secondary succession?
Building soil from bare rock takes a very long time, while secondary succession starts with soil already there.
As succession continues on a volcanic island, biodiversity usually…
More species can live there as soil deepens and more habitats form.
How do dead mosses and grasses help succession?
They decay and add nutrients to soil
Decomposing plants add organic matter, making the soil deeper and richer.
Which organisms are often the first animals to live on a new lava field?
Small animals such as insects and spiders arrive early, often blown in by wind.
What happens to pioneer species as taller plants grow?
Taller plants block light and change conditions, so pioneers are replaced over time.
Surtsey, a volcanic island near Iceland, formed in the 1960s. Scientists study it to learn about…
Surtsey began as bare lava, so it shows how life colonizes new land from the start.
Which is a sign that succession on a volcanic island is well underway?
Shrubs need deeper soil, which takes a long time to form.
Weathering breaks rock into small pieces that become part of the new soil.
Why are lichens good pioneer species?
They survive on bare rock with little water
They need large animals to spread
Lichens can live on bare rock and survive drying out, so they colonize first.
Which change in the soil happens during succession?
Weathered rock and decaying organisms build deeper, more fertile soil over time.
What would most likely grow on an old lava flow after a few hundred years?
Given enough time, soil builds up and trees can grow, forming a forest.
An old farm field slowly turns back into forest. This is…
The field still has soil, so its regrowth is secondary succession.
Which statement about the climax community is true?
It is the first to arrive
A climax community stays fairly stable until a disturbance such as fire or a storm.
sciPUN: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white (p). What colour are flowers with genotype pp?
A plant needs two recessive alleles (pp) to show the recessive white trait.
Cross Tt × Tt. What fraction of offspring are expected to be TT?
The Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt, so 1 of 4 boxes is TT.
Cross Tt × Tt. What fraction of offspring are expected to be tall (T dominant)?
TT, Tt and Tt are all tall, so 3 of the 4 boxes show the dominant trait.
Cross TT × tt. What genotype will all the offspring have?
Every offspring gets T from one parent and t from the other, so all are Tt.
Heterozygous means the two alleles are different, as in Rr.
Homozygous recessive means two recessive alleles, written as two lowercase letters.
Cross Bb × bb. What fraction of offspring are expected to be Bb?
The boxes are Bb, Bb, bb and bb, so half are Bb.
Cross RR × Rr. What fraction of offspring are expected to be rr?
The RR parent always passes on R, so no offspring can be rr.
What does a capital letter usually stand for in a Punnett square?
By convention, capital letters represent dominant alleles and lowercase letters recessive ones.
An organism's physical trait, such as eye colour, is called its…
Phenotype is the observable trait, while genotype is the allele combination.
How many boxes are in a Punnett square for one trait?
Each parent gives one of two alleles, so a one-trait Punnett square has 2 × 2 = 4 boxes.
Brown fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b). Two Bb rabbits mate. What fraction of babies are expected to be white?
Only the bb box shows white fur, which is 1 of 4 boxes.
Cross Ss × ss. What is the expected ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes?
Half the boxes are Ss (dominant) and half are ss (recessive).
Cross Gg × Gg. What is the expected ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes?
GG, Gg and Gg show the dominant trait and gg shows the recessive, giving 3 : 1.
A tall pea plant could have which genotypes (T dominant)?
Any genotype with at least one T shows the dominant tall trait.
Cross TT × TT. What fraction of offspring are expected to be short?
Both parents only pass on T, so every offspring is TT and tall.
Alleles are different forms of the same gene, such as T and t.
A recessive trait only shows when an organism has…
A single dominant allele hides the recessive one, so two recessive alleles are needed.
Yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green (y). Which genotype gives green seeds?
Green is recessive, so it appears only with two y alleles.
Cross Yy × YY. What fraction of offspring are expected to be YY?
The boxes are YY, YY, Yy and Yy, so half are YY.
Two parents with a dominant phenotype have a child with the recessive phenotype. The parents must both be…
Each parent must carry a hidden recessive allele to pass on, so both are heterozygous.
Cross Tt × tt. If 100 offspring are produced, about how many would be tall?
Half the Punnett square boxes are Tt (tall), so about 50 of 100 would be tall.
sciTaxon: Which level is broader than Class but more specific than Kingdom?
Phylum sits between Kingdom and Class.
Which level is broader than Family but more specific than Class?
Order sits between Class and Family.
Which level is broader than Species but more specific than Family?
Genus sits between Family and Species.
Animals, plants and fungi are each an example of which level?
Animalia, Plantae and Fungi are kingdoms.
Which is the broadest level of classification?
Domain is the top, broadest level that contains the most kinds of organisms.
Which level comes right before Species (from broadest to most specific)?
Genus is the level just above Species.
Which level comes right before Family (from broadest to most specific)?
Order is the level just above Family.
Which level comes right before Class (from broadest to most specific)?
Phylum is the level just above Class.
In the scientific name Ursus americanus (black bear), what is Ursus?
A scientific name is written as genus then species, so Ursus is the genus.
A scientific name like Castor canadensis (beaver) is made of which two levels?
Binomial names give the genus followed by the species.
Which scientist created the two-part naming system for species?
Carl Linnaeus developed binomial nomenclature in the 1700s.
As you move from Kingdom toward Species, the organisms in each group become…
Lower levels contain fewer kinds of organisms that share more characteristics.
Which level contains the most different kinds of organisms?
Of these choices, Kingdom is the broadest, so it includes the most kinds of organisms.
Humans and chimpanzees are in the same family but different genera. Which level do they NOT share?
Being in different genera means they split at the Genus level while sharing all broader levels.
Wolves and domestic dogs share the genus Canis. Which other level must they also share?
Organisms in the same genus must also be in the same family and all broader levels.
How many main levels are in the classification system from Domain to Species?
The levels are Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
Which of these is the correct order from broadest to most specific?
Class contains orders, and each order contains families.
Which of these is the correct order from broadest to most specific?
Kingdom is broader than Phylum, which is broader than Class.
Which of these is the correct order from most specific to broadest?
Going upward from Species, the next levels are Genus and then Family.
Which level comes two steps after Order (from broadest to most specific)?
Order is followed by Family and then Genus.
A memory trick for the levels is "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup." What does "Came" stand for?
The words match Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, so Came is Class.
Two organisms in the same order must also be in the same…
Each order belongs to one class, so sharing an order means sharing the class too.
sciCellFn: Which cell part releases energy from food through cellular respiration?
Mitochondria break down sugar to release energy the cell can use.
Which cell part captures light energy to make food?
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Which cell part contains DNA and controls cell activities?
The nucleus holds the genetic material that directs the cell's activities.
Which cell part gives a plant cell a rigid shape and support?
The tough cell wall outside the membrane supports and protects plant cells.
Which cell part stores water, food and wastes?
Vacuoles are storage sacs; plant cells have a large central vacuole full of water.
Which cell part contains enzymes that break down wastes and worn-out parts?
Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes that break down unwanted materials.
Which part is the jelly-like fluid that fills the cell and holds organelles?
Cytoplasm surrounds the organelles and is where many reactions happen.
Which part inside the nucleus makes ribosomes?
The nucleolus is a dense region of the nucleus that builds ribosomes.
Which cell part is called the powerhouse of the cell?
Mitochondria release most of the cell's usable energy.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum looks bumpy because it is covered with…
Ribosomes attached to rough ER make proteins that the ER then transports.
Which cell part surrounds the nucleus and has pores?
The nuclear membrane (envelope) encloses the nucleus and has pores for materials to pass.
Which structure helps an animal cell divide by forming spindle fibres?
Centrioles help organize the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes during division.
A wilted plant has cells that have lost water from which part?
When the central vacuole loses water, cells lose pressure and the plant wilts.
Which cell part would be most common in a muscle cell that needs lots of energy?
Cells that use a lot of energy, like muscle cells, have many mitochondria.
Which cell part is selectively permeable?
The cell membrane lets some substances through and blocks others.
Which green pigment inside chloroplasts absorbs light?
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy used in photosynthesis.
Which cell part modifies proteins and sends them out in small sacs called vesicles?
The Golgi apparatus processes, packages and ships proteins in vesicles.
Which cell part makes lipids and has no ribosomes on it?
Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids such as fats.
Which cell part would be missing in a root cell that grows underground?
Root cells get no light, so they usually have no chloroplasts.
Which structure is a network of fibres that gives the cell shape and helps it move?
The cytoskeleton is a framework of protein fibres inside the cytoplasm.
Where in the cell does photosynthesis happen?
Which cell part holds the instructions for making all of the cell's proteins?
The DNA in the nucleus carries the instructions, and ribosomes follow them to make proteins.
sciCellCmp: Which cells have a nuclear membrane?
Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic, so their nucleus is enclosed by a membrane.
Which cells carry out cellular respiration?
Plant and animal cells both break down sugar in mitochondria to release energy.
Only plant cells contain chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens.
Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus containing a nucleolus.
Which cells store starch made from their own sugar?
Plant cells store the sugar they make as starch; animal cells store glycogen instead.
Both plant and animal cells are filled with cytoplasm.
Which cells have a Golgi apparatus?
Both plant and animal cells package proteins with a Golgi apparatus.
Both plant and animal cells use endoplasmic reticulum to make and move materials.
Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts, which only plant cells have.
Which cells have a wall made of cellulose?
Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; animal cells have no cell wall.
Which shape is typical of a plant cell?
The rigid cell wall gives plant cells a box-like shape.
Why do animal cells have no fixed shape?
Without a rigid cell wall, the flexible membrane lets animal cells change shape.
Which part is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
Only plant cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Which part is found in both plant and animal cells?
All cells have a cell membrane, but the other parts are only in plant cells.
Which part is usually found in animal cells but rarely in plant cells?
Centrioles help animal cells divide; most plant cells lack them.
How do the vacuoles of plant and animal cells compare?
Plant cells have one large one
Animal cells have one large one
Both have one very large one
Plant cells have one large central vacuole; animal cells have small ones if any.
How is a plant cell's outer boundary different from an animal cell's?
It has a wall outside the membrane
It has a membrane outside the wall
It has no membrane at all
It has no boundary at all
Plant cells have a cell wall outside their cell membrane, while animal cells have only the membrane.
How do plant and animal cells get their energy differently?
Plant cells can make their own food
Animal cells can make their own food
Plant cells make sugar by photosynthesis, while animal cells must take in food; both use mitochondria.
Which statement about mitochondria is true?
Plant and animal cells both have them
Both cell types use mitochondria to release energy from sugar.
A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. It could be a…
Only plant cells have cell walls, and root cells lack chloroplasts because they get no light.
A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria and centrioles, but no cell wall. It is most likely…
No cell wall and having centrioles both point to an animal cell.
Which pair of parts would tell you a cell is from a plant?
Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not animal cells.
sciXsRCIntro: What type of rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock?
Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change rocks without melting them.
What type of rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented together?
Sedimentary rocks form from compacted and cemented sediments.
Magma is molten rock underground; it is called lava once it reaches the surface.
Which process moves rock pieces from one place to another?
Erosion carries weathered pieces away by water, wind, ice or gravity.
What must happen to a rock for it to become magma?
Rocks become magma when they get hot enough to melt deep underground.
Granite is an example of which type of rock?
Granite forms when magma cools slowly underground.
Sandstone is an example of which type of rock?
Sandstone forms from grains of sand that are pressed and cemented together.
Marble is an example of which type of rock?
Marble forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
What can sedimentary rock become after being buried deep and squeezed?
Heat and pressure deep underground change sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock.
What happens to sediments before they become sedimentary rock?
Layers of sediment are pressed together and glued by minerals to form rock.
Which source of energy drives melting and metamorphism in the rock cycle?
Heat from inside Earth melts rocks and changes them under pressure.
Which source of energy drives weathering and erosion at the surface?
Sunlight drives weather, wind and the water cycle that wear down and move rock.
What type of rock forms when magma cools slowly underground?
Slow cooling underground gives crystals time to grow large.
Why do rocks formed from lava often have tiny crystals?
Fast cooling at the surface leaves little time for crystals to grow.
Which is NOT one of the three main rock types?
The three main rock types are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Can an igneous rock become a sedimentary rock?
Igneous rock can be broken into sediment, which later forms sedimentary rock.
Can a metamorphic rock become an igneous rock?
Yes, if it melts and cools
No, it can only stay metamorphic
Only if fossils form in it
If metamorphic rock melts into magma and cools, it becomes igneous rock.
Where are sediments most often deposited?
At the bottom of lakes and oceans
Water carries sediments and drops them in calm places like lake and ocean floors.
Which rock is made of shells and skeletons of sea creatures?
Limestone is a sedimentary rock that often forms from shells and skeletons.
Slate forms when which rock is changed by heat and pressure?
Shale, a sedimentary rock, becomes slate through metamorphism.
What do we call the slow, ongoing changes of rocks from one type into another?
The rock cycle describes how rocks change between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic types.
How long do most rock cycle changes take?
Most rock cycle processes, like burial and metamorphism, are extremely slow.
sciDrift: Fossils of the plant Glossopteris are found in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. This suggests these lands…
were connected by bridges of ice
The seeds of Glossopteris could not cross oceans, so the continents must once have been joined.
Coal, which forms from swampy forests, has been found in Antarctica. This suggests Antarctica…
was once in a warmer location
Coal forms from warm-climate plants, so Antarctica must have been closer to the equator long ago.
Scratches left by ancient glaciers are found in parts of Africa and India that are now warm. This supports the idea that…
Glaciers left these marks when the continents were joined near the South Pole, before they drifted.
Why did most scientists at first reject Wegener's idea of continental drift?
He could not explain what moved the continents
He had no fossil evidence at all
He said the Earth was flat
He thought the oceans were rising
Wegener had evidence that continents moved, but no accepted mechanism for how they moved.
Who proposed the idea of sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s?
Harry Hess suggested that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward.
Matching stripes of magnetic rock on both sides of a mid-ocean ridge show that…
new sea floor forms and spreads
the ridge is made of iron
Rock records Earth's magnetic field as it forms, so mirror-image stripes show spreading from the ridge.
Which Canadian scientist helped develop plate tectonics with ideas about hot spots and transform faults?
J. Tuzo Wilson, a Canadian geophysicist, explained hot spot island chains and transform faults.
Mountains in eastern North America match mountains of the same age and rock type in…
The Appalachians match old mountains in the British Isles and Scandinavia that were joined in Pangaea.
Pangaea first split into which two large landmasses?
Pangaea broke into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south.
About how fast do tectonic plates move?
Plates move only a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
Which tool lets scientists measure plate movement directly today?
GPS receivers on the ground track tiny changes in position over years.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes are found…
in the middle of every plate
The pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes outlines the edges of the plates.
Fossils of the reptile Lystrosaurus are found in Africa, India and Antarctica. Why is this evidence of drift?
It could not swim across oceans
It lived only in deep oceans
It lived only in very cold places
A land animal could not cross wide oceans, so these lands must have been connected.
The layer under the plates that flows slowly and lets them move is the…
The plates of the lithosphere move over the soft, slowly flowing asthenosphere.
The rigid outer layer broken into tectonic plates is the…
The lithosphere, made of crust and upper mantle, is broken into plates.
Sediment on the ocean floor is thinnest…
Rock at the ridges is new, so it has had little time to collect sediment.
Wegener's theory of continental drift was published in about…
Wegener published his ideas in 1915 in a book on the origin of continents and oceans.
In which direction is the Atlantic Ocean changing in size?
Sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushes the Americas away from Europe and Africa.
Which observation shows that Hawaii's islands formed as a plate moved over a hot spot?
The islands get older in a line
All the islands are the same age
The islands are made of granite
As the Pacific Plate moves, each new island forms over the hot spot, leaving older ones farther away.
Rocks of the same type and age line up across the Atlantic in Brazil and western Africa. This suggests…
the rocks were carried by rivers
Matching rock formations on separate continents show they were once one landmass.
The theory that Earth's outer layer is made of moving plates is called…
Plate tectonics combines continental drift and sea-floor spreading into one theory.
Where is old ocean floor destroyed as plates move?
At subduction zones, ocean plates sink back into the mantle, balancing new crust made at ridges.
sciXsPlateLbl: Which boundary is shown when two plates slide past each other sideways?
At transform boundaries, plates grind past each other horizontally.
Which boundary is shown when two plates move toward each other?
Convergent boundaries are where plates collide or one sinks beneath another.
What is the zone called where one plate sinks beneath another?
In a subduction zone, the denser plate dives down into the mantle.
Which plate usually sinks when an ocean plate meets a continental plate?
The ocean plate, because it is denser
The continental plate, because it is denser
Both plates, at the same speed
Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so it subducts.
What landform is a long, narrow, very deep valley in the ocean floor at a subduction zone?
Trenches form where one plate bends down beneath another.
What kind of mountains form when rock layers are squeezed and bent at a collision?
Compression at convergent boundaries folds rock layers into mountains.
A line of volcanoes on land next to an ocean trench is called a…
Melting of the sinking plate feeds a curved line of volcanoes called a volcanic arc.
A chain of islands that gets older in one direction most likely formed over a…
A plate moving over a fixed hot spot leaves a line of volcanoes of increasing age.
An underwater mountain chain with a crack down its centre is a…
Mid-ocean ridges form where plates pull apart and magma rises to make new crust.
Which feature is found at a transform boundary?
Plates sliding past each other create long faults with frequent earthquakes.
Why do volcanoes form above subduction zones?
The sinking plate helps rock melt
Water from the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the mantle, forming magma that rises.
Which boundary usually has volcanoes, deep trenches and strong earthquakes?
Subduction of an ocean plate under a continent produces trenches, volcanoes and big earthquakes.
Why are there few volcanoes where two continental plates collide?
The plates are too cold to move
Continental crust is too light to subduct deeply, so little magma forms; mountains rise instead.
What fills the gap where two plates pull apart at a ridge?
Magma that cools into new crust
Magma rises into the gap, cools and forms new oceanic crust.
Which type of boundary is also called a constructive boundary because crust is made there?
New crust forms at divergent boundaries, so they are called constructive.
Which type of boundary destroys crust as one plate sinks?
At convergent subduction zones, crust sinks into the mantle and is destroyed.
At which boundary is crust neither made nor destroyed?
At transform boundaries, plates only slide past each other.
What is the point inside Earth where an earthquake starts called?
The focus is where rock first breaks; the epicentre is the point on the surface above it.
A diagram shows arrows pointing away from each other at a crack in the ocean floor. Which feature is it?
Plates moving apart under the ocean form a mid-ocean ridge.
A diagram shows arrows pointing toward each other and one plate going under the other. Which feature forms at the bend?
Where one plate bends down beneath another, a deep trench forms.
A diagram shows arrows pointing opposite ways along a straight line on land. What does it label?
Opposite sideways motion along a line is a transform fault.
What is the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's starting point?
The epicentre lies directly above the focus.
sciXsPlateWld: The Hawaiian Islands formed mainly over a…
Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific Plate above a hot spot.
The Mariana Trench formed at a…
The Pacific Plate sinks beneath another plate there, forming the deepest trench.
The Alps in Europe formed where…

The Red Sea is slowly widening at a…
The Arabian Plate is pulling away from Africa, widening the Red Sea.
The Queen Charlotte Fault, off Haida Gwaii in British Columbia, is mainly a…

Which small plate sinks beneath North America off the coast of British Columbia?

Mount St. Helens and the other Cascade volcanoes formed because…
an ocean plate subducts beneath North America
two plates pull apart in Washington
a hot spot sits under the volcanoes
Melting above the subducting Juan de Fuca Plate feeds the Cascade volcanoes.
Most of Canada sits on which tectonic plate?
Canada lies almost entirely on the North American Plate.
Iceland is being pulled apart by which two plates?
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through Iceland, separating the North American and Eurasian plates.
The Andes form where which plate sinks beneath South America?
The oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate.
The Aleutian Islands of Alaska are an island arc formed by…
The Pacific Plate sinking under the North American Plate created the arc of volcanic islands.
Why is Mount Everest still getting slightly taller?
A hot spot pushes it upward
Glaciers add rock to its top
The ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates continues to lift the Himalayas.
The strongest earthquake ever recorded, in Chile in 1960, happened at a…
It struck where the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America.
The East Pacific Rise is an example of a…
The East Pacific Rise is a mid-ocean ridge where plates spread apart.
Yellowstone National Park sits above a…
Yellowstone's geysers and past eruptions come from a hot spot under the North American Plate.
Why are earthquakes common in California?
Two plates slide past each other there
A hot spot lies under it
It sits in the middle of a plate
The Pacific Plate grinds past the North American Plate along the San Andreas Fault.
Which country is crossed by the North Anatolian Fault, a major transform boundary?
The North Anatolian Fault in Turkey is a transform fault with frequent earthquakes.
Mount Fuji in Japan formed mainly because of…
Japan's volcanoes form above plates that subduct beneath it.
The Ring of Fire is mostly made of which kind of boundary?
Most of the Ring of Fire is subduction zones that produce volcanoes and earthquakes.
The Atlantic coast of Canada is quiet geologically because it…
is far from any plate boundary
Eastern Canada is in the middle of the North American Plate, away from active boundaries.
Which plate is moving north into Asia to form the Himalayas?
The Indian Plate's collision with the Eurasian Plate built the Himalayas.
The Great Rift Valley in East Africa may one day become…
As the African continent splits apart, seawater may eventually flood the rift, as it did in the Red Sea.
sciXsWCSel: Which process returns water from clouds to Earth's surface?
Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
A puddle disappears on a sunny afternoon. Which process happened?
Heat from the Sun turned the liquid water into water vapour.
Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass of juice. Which process is this?
Water vapour in the air cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid.
Rainwater flows over a parking lot into a storm drain. Which process is this?
Water that flows over the ground surface instead of soaking in is runoff.
Which process turns water vapour directly into frost on a cold window?
Deposition is when a gas changes straight into a solid, as when vapour forms frost.
Snow on a mountain turns into liquid water in spring. Which process is this?
Melting changes solid ice or snow into liquid water.
What provides the energy that drives the water cycle?
Sunlight heats water and causes evaporation, which keeps the cycle moving.
Where is most of Earth's water found?
About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans.
An underground layer of rock or gravel that holds water is called…
Aquifers store groundwater in the spaces in rock, sand or gravel.
Fog forming over a lake on a cool morning is an example of…
Fog is tiny water droplets made when water vapour cools near the ground.
Water absorbed by tree roots exits through tiny holes in the leaves. Which process is this?
Transpiration is the release of water vapour from plant leaves.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a lake up to a cloud. What process does it show?
Water moving from a lake into the air as vapour is evaporation.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a cloud down to a mountain. What process does it show?
Water falling from a cloud to the ground is precipitation.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a hillside into the soil below. What process does it show?
Water soaking down into the ground is infiltration.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a tree's leaves up into the air. What process does it show?
Water vapour leaving plant leaves is transpiration.
Snow falling on the Prairies in January is an example of…
Snow is a form of precipitation falling from clouds.
Which process is more likely on a paved road than on a grassy field?
Pavement stops water from soaking in, so more of it runs off the surface.
Rain falling on a forest soaks into loose soil. Which process is this?
Infiltration is water entering and moving down into the soil.
Snow slowly shrinks on a cold, sunny, windy day without melting. Which process is this?
Sublimation is solid ice changing directly into water vapour.
Which process makes water vapour turn into tiny cloud droplets high in the sky?
As air rises and cools, water vapour condenses into droplets that form clouds.
Melted snow flowing downhill into a river in spring is an example of…
Meltwater moving over the surface into streams and rivers is runoff.
What do we call water stored below ground that fills spaces in soil and rock?
Groundwater is water held underground in soil and rock.
sciXsCarbon: In which form is carbon found in the atmosphere?
Most carbon in the air is in the gas carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>.
How do animals get the carbon they need to build their bodies?
By eating plants or other animals
By soaking it up from sunlight
Consumers get carbon compounds from the food they eat.
Which process releases carbon dioxide when living things use food for energy?
Cellular respiration breaks down sugar and releases CO<sub>2</sub> as a waste product.
Fossil fuels such as coal and oil formed from…
the remains of ancient living things
Buried plants and tiny sea organisms were changed by heat and pressure over millions of years.
Which organisms break down dead matter and release carbon back to the air and soil?
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and release CO<sub>2</sub>.
Which natural event releases carbon from deep inside Earth into the air?
Volcanoes release carbon dioxide gas from Earth's interior.
shells and skeletons of sea creatures
Sea creatures build shells from carbon compounds, which pile up and become limestone.
Which gas, produced by burning fossil fuels, traps heat in the atmosphere?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat and warms Earth.
What happens to ocean water as it absorbs more carbon dioxide?
CO<sub>2</sub> reacts with water to form carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH.
Which Canadian ecosystem stores large amounts of carbon in its trees, peat and soil?
Canada's boreal forest and peatlands hold huge amounts of carbon in plants and soil.
Which pair of processes are opposites in the carbon cycle?
Photosynthesis takes in CO<sub>2</sub>, while respiration releases it.
In photosynthesis, plants combine carbon dioxide and water to make…
Plants use light energy to turn CO<sub>2</sub> and water into glucose and oxygen.
Which of these is a carbon source rather than a carbon sink?
Burning coal releases more carbon than it stores, so it is a source.
Which action would help reduce the amount of carbon dioxide added to the air?
Using transit instead of a car burns less fuel, so less CO<sub>2</sub> is released.
Which holds more carbon: the oceans or the atmosphere?
The oceans store many times more carbon than the atmosphere.
Why does thawing permafrost in northern Canada worry scientists?
It removes carbon from the air
As frozen soil thaws, microbes break down old plant matter and release CO<sub>2</sub> and methane.
Carbon atoms in a maple leaf came most directly from…
Plants build their tissues from carbon taken from CO<sub>2</sub> during photosynthesis.
Which carbon-containing gas is released by cows during digestion?
Microbes in a cow's stomach produce methane, which is also a greenhouse gas.
Burning a log in a campfire releases carbon as…
Combustion combines the carbon in wood with oxygen to make CO<sub>2</sub>.
Which part of a living thing is made from carbon compounds?
Sugars, fats, proteins and DNA are all built around carbon atoms.
Why do carbon dioxide levels in the air rise slightly in the Northern Hemisphere winter?
Leaves fall and plants slow down in winter, so less CO<sub>2</sub> is taken from the air.
What is the movement of carbon between the air, living things, oceans and rocks called?
The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves among Earth's reservoirs.
sciATM: Which layer is the coldest, reaching about −90 °C at its top?
The mesosphere is the coldest layer because it has little ozone to absorb sunlight and is far from the warm ground.
In the troposphere, what usually happens to the temperature as you go higher?
The troposphere is heated from the ground up, so the air gets colder with height.
Why does the temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet light from the Sun
Clouds trap heat from the ground there
Nitrogen there burns and releases heat
Jet engines release heat in that layer
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs the Sun's UV rays and warms the upper part of the layer.
What happens to air pressure as you climb higher in the atmosphere?
Higher up there is less air above you pressing down, so air pressure drops.
Which layer holds about three-quarters of the mass of the atmosphere?
Gravity pulls most air close to the ground, so the thin troposphere holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass.
What is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere called?
The tropopause marks the top of the troposphere, where the stratosphere begins.
Which gas makes up a little under 1% of Earth's atmosphere?
Argon is the third most common gas in dry air, at about 0.9%.
Which gas makes up only about 0.04% of the air but helps trap heat near Earth?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat even though it is a tiny part of the air.
In which layer can temperatures pass 1000 °C, even though the air is too thin to feel hot?
The thermosphere absorbs intense solar radiation, so its few particles are very hot.
Which list orders the layers from Earth's surface upward?
Going up from the ground, the layers are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and then the exosphere.
In which layer do almost all clouds and rain form?
Nearly all water vapour is in the troposphere, so clouds and precipitation form there.
Which layer reaches the farthest, up to about 10 000 km above Earth?
The exosphere is the very thin outermost layer that slowly fades into space.
Why is it harder to breathe on top of a very high mountain?
The air is thinner, so each breath has less oxygen
The air there is mostly carbon dioxide instead
Oxygen sinks down into the rocks below
The ozone layer blocks oxygen at that height
Air pressure is lower up high, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.
On average, about how high does the troposphere reach?
The troposphere extends roughly 8 to 15 km up, about 12 km on average.
The ozone layer protects living things by absorbing most of the Sun's …
Ozone absorbs most harmful UV radiation before it reaches the ground.
Which layer lies directly above the stratosphere?
Going upward, the mesosphere comes right after the stratosphere.
Which layer lies directly below the exosphere?
The thermosphere is the layer just beneath the outermost exosphere.
Which layer lies directly above the troposphere?
The stratosphere starts at the tropopause, right above the troposphere.
Weather balloons often rise to about 30 km before they burst. Which layer is that?
The stratosphere runs from about 12 km to 50 km, so 30 km is inside it.
About what percent of Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen?
Nitrogen is the most common gas in the air, at about 78%.
What keeps the atmosphere held around Earth instead of drifting into space?
Earth's gravity pulls on the gas particles and holds the atmosphere in place.
Long-distance passenger jets often cruise just above the weather, in the lowest part of which layer?
Jets can fly in the lower stratosphere, above most of the clouds and storms of the troposphere.
sciNWT: Which of Newton's laws explains this? A swimmer pushes water backward and glides forward.
The swimmer pushes on the water and the water pushes back on the swimmer with an equal and opposite force.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A soccer ball kicked harder speeds up more.
A larger net force on the same mass gives a larger acceleration, as F = ma says.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A tablecloth yanked quickly from under dishes leaves the dishes in place.
The dishes have inertia and tend to stay at rest when the cloth is pulled away quickly.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? Seatbelts stop riders from flying forward when a car stops suddenly.
Riders keep moving forward because of inertia unless a force, like a seatbelt, stops them.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A balloon zooms forward as air rushes out of its back.
The balloon pushes air backward and the air pushes the balloon forward.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A truck needs a much larger engine force than a car to reach the same acceleration.
A larger mass needs a larger force for the same acceleration, as F = ma says.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A hockey puck slides a long way across smooth ice.
With very little friction, the puck keeps moving at nearly the same speed because of inertia.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? When you jump, you push down on the ground and the ground pushes you up.
Your push on the ground is matched by an equal and opposite push from the ground on you.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? A coin on a card over a cup drops into the cup when the card is flicked away.
The coin's inertia keeps it in place while the card moves, so gravity then pulls it into the cup.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? Paddling backward on the water moves a canoe forward.
The paddle pushes water backward and the water pushes the canoe forward.
Which of Newton's laws explains this? An astronaut in space throws a tool forward and drifts backward.
The astronaut pushes the tool forward and the tool pushes the astronaut backward with an equal force.
A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg box. What is its acceleration?
Using a = F ÷ m, 20 N ÷ 4 kg = 5 m/s².
What net force is needed to accelerate a 1000 kg car at 2 m/s²?
Using F = ma, 1000 kg × 2 m/s² = 2000 N.
A 0.5 kg ball accelerates at 10 m/s². What net force acts on it?
Using F = ma, 0.5 kg × 10 m/s² = 5 N.
A net force of 30 N gives an object an acceleration of 6 m/s². What is its mass?
Using m = F ÷ a, 30 N ÷ 6 m/s² = 5 kg.
An object's resistance to changes in its motion
The force that pulls objects toward Earth
The speed at which an object is travelling
The rubbing force between two surfaces
Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep doing what it is already doing.
Which object has the most inertia?
Inertia depends on mass, and the loaded truck has by far the most mass.
How do the two forces in an action–reaction pair compare?
Equal in size and opposite in direction
Equal in size and in the same direction
Unequal, with the action force larger
Unequal, with the reaction force larger
Newton's third law says the forces in a pair are always equal and opposite.
Why don't action–reaction forces cancel each other out?
They act on the same object
They are not equal in size
They point in the same direction
Forces only cancel when they act on the same object, and each force in a pair acts on a different object.
The net force on a moving object becomes zero. What does the object do?
Keeps moving at a constant velocity
Speeds up at a steady rate
By the first law, with no net force an object keeps its speed and direction.
The same force is applied to an object with twice the mass. What happens to its acceleration?
Since a = F ÷ m, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
What is the SI unit of force, equal to 1 kg·m/s²?
One newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
sciXsTransW: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed?

A wave travels at 20 m/s with a wavelength of 4 m. What is its frequency?
A wave travels at 30 m/s with a frequency of 10 Hz. What is its wavelength?
What is the SI unit of frequency?
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), meaning waves per second.
In which unit is wavelength measured?
Wavelength is a distance, so it is measured in metres.
A wave has a period of 0.5 s. What is its frequency?
Which of these is NOT a transverse wave?

Sound in air is a longitudinal wave, where particles vibrate back and forth along the wave's direction.
Which of these is a transverse wave?
Microwaves are electromagnetic waves, which are transverse.
You shake a rope with bigger up-and-down motions. What happens to the energy the wave carries?
A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy.
The middle line that a transverse wave moves above and below is the…

Ten waves pass a point in 2 s. What is the frequency?
What does a transverse wave carry from one place to another?

Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave A has the higher frequency. Wave A has the…

S (secondary) waves shake the ground side to side, perpendicular to their direction of travel.
Through which can S waves, the transverse earthquake waves, travel?

A crest and the next trough are 1.5 m apart, measured along the wave. What is the wavelength?

What is the period of a wave?
The time for one complete wave to pass
The height of a crest above rest
The number of crests in a metre
The period is the time for one full wave cycle, measured in seconds.
A water wave moves at 2 m/s with a frequency of 0.5 Hz. What is its wavelength?
Shaking a rope more times each second increases the wave's…
More waves made per second means a higher frequency.
sciWaveP: Wave A has a wavelength of 2 m and wave B has a wavelength of 5 m. Both travel at the same speed. Which has the higher frequency?
At equal speeds, the wave with the shorter wavelength has the higher frequency.
Two sounds travel through air: one at 200 Hz and one at 800 Hz. Which has the longer wavelength?

A wave's amplitude doubles but nothing else changes. What happens to its frequency?
Amplitude and frequency are separate properties, so changing one does not change the other.
Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, about 700 nm.
Which colour of visible light has the highest frequency?
Violet light has the shortest wavelength and therefore the highest frequency of visible light.
A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
A whisper and a shout are at the same pitch. Which property mainly differs?
Loudness depends on amplitude, so the shout has a larger amplitude.
A dog whistle is too high-pitched for people to hear. Compared with everyday sounds, its waves have a…

The frequency of a wave is halved while its speed stays the same. What happens to its wavelength?

Which ocean wave carries more energy?

Wave A has crests 4 cm apart. Wave B has crests 8 cm apart. Which has the longer wavelength?

B's amplitude is four times A's

For electromagnetic waves, a higher frequency means…
Higher-frequency electromagnetic waves, like X-rays, carry more energy than low-frequency ones like radio.
A 10 Hz wave and a 20 Hz wave travel on the same string at the same speed. How does the 20 Hz wave's wavelength compare?
Doubling the frequency at the same speed halves the wavelength.
A guitarist plucks the same string harder. What changes about the sound wave?
Plucking harder makes bigger vibrations, increasing amplitude and loudness, not pitch.
Pressing a guitar string against a fret makes the note higher. What has increased?
A shorter vibrating string vibrates faster, raising the frequency and pitch.
Which has the shorter wavelength: radio waves or X-rays?
X-rays have wavelengths far shorter than radio waves, which can be metres long.
A wave has a period of 0.1 s. What is its frequency?
Wave A has a frequency of 5 Hz and wave B has 15 Hz. Which has the shorter period?
Period = 1 ÷ frequency, so the higher-frequency wave has the shorter period.
A wave enters a medium where it travels twice as fast, but its frequency stays the same. Its wavelength…
Since wavelength = speed ÷ frequency, doubling the speed doubles the wavelength.
Which wave has the greatest amplitude?
One with crests 5 cm above rest
One with crests 2 cm above rest
One with crests 1 cm above rest
One with crests 3 cm above rest
Amplitude is the height of the crest above rest, and 5 cm is the greatest.
