Which plant cell part does this? Found in leaf cells but not in root cells, which get no light
Root cells do not receive light, so they lack chloroplasts, while leaf cells have many.
Which plant cell part does this? Stores sugars, salts and pigments in a sac of cell sap
The central vacuole is filled with cell sap that stores water, sugars, salts and some pigments.
Which plant cell part does this? Releases energy in the cells of both leaves and roots
All living plant cells respire, so mitochondria are found in roots as well as leaves.
Which plant cell part does this? Directs cell division by copying and passing on DNA
The nucleus copies its DNA so each new cell receives a full set of instructions.
Which plant cell part does this? Shrinks when the plant loses too much water
When a plant lacks water, the vacuole loses water and shrinks, so the plant wilts.
Which plant cell part does this? Freely lets water through but gives the cell its boxy shape
The cell wall is fully permeable but rigid, giving plant cells their regular, box-like shape.
Which plant cell part does this? Contains its own DNA and stacks of membranes called thylakoids
Chloroplasts have stacks of thylakoid membranes where light is captured, plus a small amount of their own DNA.
Which plant cell part does this? Keeps the cell's contents inside while letting oxygen in
The cell membrane holds the cell contents in while allowing small molecules such as oxygen to pass.
Which plant cell part does this? Site where many chemical reactions take place, outside the organelles
Many of the cell's reactions happen in the cytoplasm around the organelles.
Which plant cell part does this? Has a folded inner membrane where most ATP is made
The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into cristae, where most ATP is produced.
Which plant cell part does this? Contains the nucleolus, which helps make ribosomes
The nucleolus, found inside the nucleus, builds the parts of ribosomes.
Which plant cell part does this? Gives off oxygen as a by-product in sunlight
During photosynthesis in chloroplasts, water is split and oxygen is released.
sciXsAnCellF: Which animal cell part does this? Holds the chromosomes and directs cell activities
The nucleus contains the chromosomes, whose DNA controls the cell's activities.
Which animal cell part does this? Uses oxygen to release energy from glucose
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, using oxygen to release energy from glucose.
Which animal cell part does this? Thin, flexible outer boundary of the cell
Animal cells have no cell wall, so the flexible cell membrane is their outer boundary.
Which animal cell part does this? Builds proteins using instructions from the DNA
Ribosomes join amino acids in the order coded by the DNA to make proteins.
Which animal cell part does this? Contains digestive enzymes that break down old organelles
Lysosomes are sacs of enzymes that digest worn-out cell parts and wastes.
Which animal cell part does this? Fluid that holds the organelles in place
The cytoplasm fills the cell and surrounds the organelles.
Which animal cell part does this? Lets oxygen in and carbon dioxide out
Gases pass in and out of the cell through the cell membrane.
Which animal cell part does this? Found in large numbers in active muscle cells
Muscle cells need a lot of energy, so they contain many mitochondria.
Which animal cell part does this? Surrounded by an envelope with pores
The nuclear envelope has pores that let materials pass between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
Which animal cell part does this? Destroys bacteria that a white blood cell swallows
In white blood cells, lysosomes fuse with swallowed bacteria and digest them.
Which animal cell part does this? Can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER
Ribosomes either float freely or stud the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Which animal cell part does this? Has receptors that detect hormones outside the cell
Receptor proteins in the cell membrane bind to signals such as hormones.
Which animal cell part does this? Copies its DNA before the cell divides
Before division, the DNA in the nucleus is copied so each new cell gets a complete set.
Which animal cell part does this? Mostly water with dissolved salts and nutrients
The cytoplasm is mainly water containing dissolved substances the cell uses.
Which animal cell part does this? Has its own small loop of DNA and a folded inner membrane
Mitochondria contain their own DNA and have inner folds called cristae.
Which animal cell part does this? Makes the enzymes and hormones a cell sends out
Enzymes and many hormones are proteins, which are built by ribosomes.
Which animal cell part does this? Pinches in to take large particles into the cell
The cell membrane can fold around particles and bring them in, a process called endocytosis.
Which animal cell part does this? Recycles materials when a cell is starving
Lysosomes break down cell parts so their building blocks can be reused.
Which animal cell part does this? Contains the nucleolus
The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus that makes ribosome parts.
Which animal cell part does this? Gives off carbon dioxide and water as waste products
Cellular respiration in mitochondria produces carbon dioxide and water.
Which animal cell part does this? Where glycolysis, the first step of respiration, happens
Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm before the products enter the mitochondria.
Which animal cell part does this? Selectively permeable layer made of a double layer of lipids
The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer that lets some substances through but not others.
sciXsOrgBody: Muscle tissue is a group of similar muscle cells working together.
A red blood cell is a single cell; the others are larger levels of organization.
The nervous system is made of several organs, such as the brain and spinal cord, working together.
The brain, spinal cord and nerves make up the …
The brain, spinal cord and nerves carry and process signals as the nervous system.
Which organs belong to the digestive system?
The stomach and intestines break down food and absorb nutrients.
Which organs belong to the excretory system?
The kidneys filter wastes from the blood and the bladder stores urine.
Nerve tissue is made of neurons that carry electrical signals.
Which tissue can contract to cause movement?
Muscle cells shorten when they contract, causing movement.
Bone, blood and fat are all examples of which type of tissue?
Connective tissues support, connect or protect other parts of the body.
Which systems work together to let you move your arm?
Muscles pull on bones to move the arm.
Which systems work together to get nutrients from food to cells?
The digestive system breaks down food and the circulatory system carries the nutrients to cells.
Which system sends chemical messages called hormones?
Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood to control body activities.
What is the main job of the skeletal system?
To support and protect the body
Bones give the body its shape, support it and protect organs such as the brain.
Which organ is part of both the respiratory and digestive pathways?
Both air and food pass through the pharynx before going to the trachea or esophagus.
Which level of organization is the lung?
The lung is made of several tissues working together, so it is an organ.
Which level of organization is a neuron?
A neuron is a single nerve cell.
Which level of organization is the skin of your hand?
Skin is an organ made of epithelial, connective, nerve and other tissues.
Which system's main organs are the heart and blood vessels?
The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels of the circulatory system.
Keeping conditions inside the body stable
Homeostasis is how body systems work together to keep things like temperature and water balance steady.
When you get too hot, you sweat. Which system does sweat come from?
Sweat glands in the skin, part of the integumentary system, release sweat to cool you.
Which systems work together when you pull your hand away from a hot stove?
Nerves detect the heat and signal muscles to pull your hand away.
Several organ systems working together make up an …
An organism, such as a person, is made of all its organ systems working together.
sciXsHeart: Which chambers pump blood out of the heart?
The thick-walled ventricles contract to push blood out into the arteries.
Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure.
Which blood vessels carry blood back to the heart?
Veins return blood to the heart's atria.
What is the job of the valves in the heart?
To stop blood from flowing backward
To make new red blood cells
To add oxygen to the blood
To filter wastes from the blood
Heart valves close after each beat so blood flows in only one direction.
Why do many veins have valves?
Blood in veins is under low pressure and could flow backward
Veins carry blood away from the heart at high pressure
Valves add oxygen to the blood in veins
Valves make the blood in veins clot
Blood pressure in veins is low, so valves keep blood moving toward the heart.
Where does blood pick up oxygen?
Oxygen moves from the air sacs of the lungs into the blood in nearby capillaries.
Which blood vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs?
The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle and carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
Which blood vessel brings oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart?
Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
Which large veins return oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium?
The superior and inferior venae cavae bring blood from the body into the right atrium.
What do red blood cells carry?
Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which binds and carries oxygen.
What do white blood cells do?
White blood cells defend the body against germs.
A type of white blood cell
Plasma is the yellowish liquid that carries blood cells, nutrients and wastes.
Which order shows the path of blood leaving the left ventricle?
Blood leaves through the aorta into arteries, then capillaries, then returns through veins.
Why is the human circulatory system called a double loop?
Blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit
Each blood vessel has two walls
Blood is pumped twice per second
One loop goes from the heart to the lungs and back, the other from the heart to the body and back.
Which blood vessels supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen?
Coronary arteries branch off the aorta and feed the heart muscle.
A blocked coronary artery can cause a …
If a coronary artery is blocked, part of the heart muscle loses its oxygen supply and is damaged.
What happens to your heart rate during exercise?
Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver more blood.
Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
So substances can pass through them easily
So they can hold blood at high pressure
So they can pump blood like the heart
So they can store extra blood
Thin capillary walls let oxygen, nutrients and wastes move easily between blood and cells.
Which system works most closely with the circulatory system to remove carbon dioxide?
Blood carries carbon dioxide to the lungs, where the respiratory system breathes it out.
Which wall separates the left and right sides of the heart?
The septum is a muscular wall that keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart.
Which has the thickest, most muscular walls?
Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls to handle the high pressure of blood from the heart.
Which habit helps keep the heart and blood vessels healthy?
Sitting for most of the day
Regular exercise strengthens the heart and helps keep blood pressure healthy.
sciNAT: In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to pass on their genes?
Those best suited to their environment
Those that live the shortest time
Those that try hardest to change
Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, passing on more of their genes.
Where does new variation in a population ultimately come from?
Mutations create new alleles, which are the raw material for natural selection.
Giraffes stretching their necks and passing on longer necks is an idea that is …
Traits gained during life are not passed to offspring; longer necks spread because of inherited variation and selection.
Bacteria in a population that survive an antibiotic and multiply show …
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, so resistance becomes more common through natural selection.
Why should you finish a full course of antibiotics as prescribed?
To avoid leaving resistant bacteria to multiply
To make the bacteria grow faster
To make your body produce antibiotics
Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive, helping resistance spread.
Breeders choosing which dogs to mate is an example of …
When humans choose which organisms reproduce, it is called artificial or selective breeding.
What is the term for an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment?
In biology, fitness means how well an organism survives and passes on its genes.
Darwin studied finches on which islands?
Darwin observed finches with different beaks on the Galápagos Islands.
Finches on different islands had different beak shapes because …
each beak suited the food on that island
the birds chose new beaks each year
all beaks changed at random every day
beaks are shaped by the weather each morning
Birds with beaks suited to the local food survived better, so beak shapes differed between islands.
The white fur of an Arctic hare in winter helps it survive by providing …
White fur blends in with snow, making the hare harder for predators to spot.
What happens to a species if none of its members can survive a change in its environment?
If no individuals have traits that let them survive, the species dies out.
Which is an example of a structural adaptation?
The thick blubber of a seal
Blubber is a physical body feature, so it is a structural adaptation.
Which is an example of a behavioural adaptation?
The sharp claws of a lynx
The thick fur of a polar bear
The long ears of a hare
Migration is something an animal does, so it is a behavioural adaptation.
Why does natural selection need traits to be inherited?
Only inherited traits can be passed to offspring
Inherited traits never change at all
Inherited traits only appear in adults
Selection changes a population only if the helpful traits are passed from parents to offspring.
Organisms produce more offspring than can survive. This leads to …
Limited resources mean not all offspring survive, so individuals compete.
Bones with the same basic structure in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper are evidence of …
Homologous structures suggest these animals inherited the same bone pattern from a common ancestor.
Which kind of rock layer usually holds the oldest fossils?
In undisturbed rock, deeper layers formed first, so they hold older fossils.
Over many generations, natural selection changes …
Individuals do not evolve; the frequency of traits in a population changes over time.
Peppered moths became lighter again after air pollution was reduced. Why?
Light moths were better hidden on clean trees
Dark moths chose to change colour
All the moths became one colour overnight
On clean, pale bark, light moths were harder for birds to see, so they survived better.
A change in an organism's DNA
A move to a new habitat
A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence, which may produce a new trait.
Insect pests that survive a pesticide and breed show …
The survivors pass on their resistance, so over time more of the population is resistant.
Who, along with Darwin, also came up with the idea of natural selection?
Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea of natural selection at about the same time as Darwin.
sciGenVoc: AA has two identical dominant alleles, so it is homozygous dominant.
Aa has one dominant and one recessive allele, so it is heterozygous.
aa has two recessive alleles, so it is homozygous recessive.
RR has two copies of the dominant allele R.
rr has two copies of the recessive allele r.
Gg carries two different alleles, one dominant and one recessive.
TT has two identical dominant alleles.
Round seeds is an observable trait, so it is a phenotype.
Flower colour is a trait you can see, so it is a phenotype.
A blood type is a characteristic you can test for, so it is a phenotype.
Curly hair is an observable characteristic, so it is a phenotype.
Pp has one dominant P and one recessive p allele.
ee has two identical recessive alleles.
Alleles are different forms of the same gene, such as tall or short.
What does dominant, the word in bold, mean for an allele?
It shows its trait even with one copy
It shows its trait only with two copies
It is never passed to offspring
A dominant allele is expressed whenever at least one copy is present.
What does recessive, the word in bold, mean for an allele?
It shows its trait only with two copies
It shows its trait even with one copy
It blends with the other allele
A recessive allele is hidden unless an organism has two copies of it.
What is the genotype of an organism?
The alleles it has for a trait
The number of cells it has
The genotype is the genetic makeup, such as Bb, for a trait.
What is the phenotype of an organism?
The alleles it has for a trait
The letters used in a Punnett square
The phenotype is the physical or observable characteristic, such as brown eyes.
Tall (T) is dominant over short (t). What is the phenotype of a Tt plant?
The dominant T allele is expressed, so a Tt plant is tall.
Purple (P) is dominant over white (p). Which genotype gives white flowers?
Only two recessive alleles, pp, produce the recessive white phenotype.
Brown eyes (B) are dominant over blue (b). Which genotypes give brown eyes?
Any genotype with at least one dominant B allele shows brown eyes.
Two organisms both have purple flowers, but one is PP and one is Pp. They have the same …
They look the same, so they share a phenotype, but their genotypes differ.
sciXsInquiry: What is the independent variable in an experiment?
The variable the scientist changes on purpose
The variable that is measured as a result
The variable kept the same in every trial
The variable that cannot be controlled
The independent (manipulated) variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes.
What is the dependent variable in an experiment?
The variable measured to see the effect
The variable the scientist changes on purpose
The variable kept the same in every trial
The variable chosen after the results
The dependent (responding) variable is what you measure to see how it responds.
What are controlled variables?
Factors kept the same in every trial
Factors changed on purpose each trial
Results measured at the end
Guesses made before testing
Keeping other factors constant makes it a fair test of the independent variable.
A student tests how fertilizer amount affects plant height. What is the dependent variable?
Plant height
Amount of fertilizer
Type of pot used
Amount of water given
Plant height is measured to see the effect of the fertilizer.
A student tests how fertilizer amount affects plant height. What is the independent variable?
Amount of fertilizer
Plant height
Amount of sunlight
Type of soil used
The fertilizer amount is what the student changes on purpose.
Why do scientists repeat trials?
To make results more reliable
To change the hypothesis each time
To make the experiment take longer
To get the answer they want
Repeated trials reduce the effect of random errors and show whether results are consistent.
What is the purpose of a control group?
To compare results with a group that gets no treatment
To make sure every group gets the treatment
To replace the need for measurements
To decide the hypothesis after testing
A control group shows what happens without the independent variable, so effects can be compared.
Which is a testable question?
Does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?
Is blue the best colour in the world?
Why do people like summer more than winter?
Which song is the most beautiful?
A testable question can be answered by changing a variable and measuring a result.
Which hypothesis is written as a testable prediction?
If light increases, then the plant will grow taller
Plants are probably nice to have around
Light is a type of plant food for sure
Plants and light are interesting to study
An "if…then" statement predicts a measurable result of changing a variable.
What is an observation?
Information gathered using the senses or instruments
A guess made before an experiment
A theory accepted by all scientists
A rule that can never change
Observations are what you see, hear, measure or record during an investigation.
Which is a quantitative observation?
The water is 25 °C
The water looks cloudy
The water smells strange
The water feels warm
Quantitative observations involve numbers and measurements.
Which is a qualitative observation?
The solution turned blue
The solution has a mass of 40 g
The solution's volume is 50 mL
The solution is at 30 °C
Qualitative observations describe qualities like colour without using numbers.
What is an inference?
A logical explanation based on observations
A measurement taken with a tool
A list of materials needed
A drawing of the apparatus
An inference interprets observations to explain what is happening.
What is a scientific law?
A description of what always happens under certain conditions
A guess that has not been tested
An explanation that has been disproved
A rule voted on by a government
A law, like the law of conservation of mass, describes a pattern found in nature without explaining why.
Why is peer review important in science?
Other experts check the work for errors
It keeps results secret from the public
It lets scientists skip experiments
It makes every hypothesis correct
Peer review lets other scientists examine methods and conclusions before work is published.
Why should an experiment test only one independent variable at a time?
So you know what caused any change
So the experiment finishes faster
So you need fewer measurements
So the hypothesis is always supported
If several factors change at once, you cannot tell which one caused the result.
What type of graph is best for showing how a measurement changes over time?
Line graph
Pie chart
Pictograph
Venn diagram
Line graphs show trends in continuous data, such as change over time.
A conclusion should …
state whether the data support the hypothesis
repeat the list of materials
describe the safety rules
add new data that was not collected
A conclusion summarizes what the results show about the hypothesis.
A larger sample size in an experiment usually makes the results …
more reliable
less reliable
always wrong
impossible to graph
More test subjects reduce the effect of unusual individual results.
What is a source of error?
Something that may have affected the accuracy of results
The variable you change on purpose
The final answer of the experiment
The question you are trying to answer
Sources of error, like inaccurate measuring, can make results less accurate.
Which tool would you use to measure the volume of a liquid accurately?
Graduated cylinder
Thermometer
Metre stick
Balance
A graduated cylinder is marked in millilitres for measuring liquid volume.
What is a model in science?
A simplified representation of a real thing or idea
An exact copy that has no limits
A guess with no evidence behind it
A final law that cannot change
Models, like a diagram of an atom, help explain things that are too big, small or complex to see directly.
sciXsMicro: Which part of the microscope is this? The clips that hold the slide in place on the stage
Stage clips hold the slide steady so it does not move while you look.
Which part of the microscope is this? The rotating part that holds the objective lenses
Turning the revolving nosepiece switches between objective lenses.
Which part of the microscope is this? The curved part you hold with one hand when carrying it
You carry a microscope by the arm, with your other hand under the base.
Which part of the microscope is this? The flat bottom that supports the whole microscope
The base keeps the microscope steady and supports it from underneath.
Which part of the microscope is this? The lamp or mirror under the stage that sends light up through the slide
The light source shines up through the specimen so you can see it.
Which part of the microscope is this? The tube that connects the eyepiece to the objective lenses
The body tube holds the eyepiece at the right distance from the objectives.
Which part of the microscope is this? The shortest objective lens, used first to find the specimen
You start with the low-power objective because it has the widest field of view.
Which part of the microscope is this? The longest objective lens, which magnifies the most
The high-power objective is longest and gives the greatest magnification.
Which part of the microscope is this? The knob you should never use with the high-power objective
The coarse knob moves the stage a lot and could crack the slide against the high-power lens.
Which part of the microscope is this? The knob used to make small focus adjustments
The fine focus knob moves the stage only slightly for sharp focus.
Which part of the microscope is this? The platform with a hole in the middle for light to pass through
The stage has an opening so light from below can pass through the slide.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part you adjust to make the image brighter or dimmer
Opening or closing the diaphragm changes how much light reaches the specimen.
Which part of the microscope is this? The lens closest to your eye
The eyepiece, or ocular lens, is at the top of the body tube where you look in.
Which part of the microscope is this? The lens under the stage that focuses light onto the specimen
The condenser gathers and focuses light from the source onto the slide.
Which part of the microscope is this? The lenses closest to the slide
Objective lenses sit just above the slide on the nosepiece.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part whose magnification is multiplied by the objective to give total magnification
Total magnification equals eyepiece magnification times objective magnification.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part you turn to click a different objective into place
Rotating the nosepiece swaps objectives until one clicks into position.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part you should hold underneath while carrying the microscope
Supporting the base with one hand keeps the microscope from tipping or dropping.
Which part of the microscope is this? The 40× lens used to see small details
The 40× objective is the high-power lens used to see fine detail.
Which part of the microscope is this? The knob used first, at low power, to bring the specimen roughly into view
At low power you first use the coarse focus knob to find the specimen.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part that holds the body tube above the base and stage
The arm connects the upper parts of the microscope to the base.
Which part of the microscope is this? The part you turn off or unplug before putting the microscope away
The light source uses electricity, so it should be switched off and unplugged after use.
sciBondT: What type of bond holds the atoms together in LiF ?
Lithium is a metal and fluorine is a non-metal, so electrons are transferred to form ions.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in Na₂O ?
Sodium (a metal) gives electrons to oxygen (a non-metal), forming an ionic compound.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in CaCl₂ ?
Calcium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so they form an ionic bond.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in K₂S ?
Potassium transfers electrons to sulfur, a non-metal, forming ions.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in BaO ?
Barium is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal, so the bond is ionic.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in MgCl₂ ?
Magnesium loses electrons to chlorine, forming Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in SrBr₂ ?
Strontium is a metal and bromine is a non-metal, so the bond is ionic.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in N₂ ?
Two nitrogen atoms are both non-metals, so they share electrons.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in Cl₂ ?
Two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in SO₂ ?
Sulfur and oxygen are both non-metals, so they share electrons.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in CCl₄ ?
Carbon and chlorine are non-metals, so their atoms are joined by shared electrons.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in PCl₃ ?
Phosphorus and chlorine are both non-metals, forming covalent bonds.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in CS₂ ?
Carbon and sulfur are non-metals, so the molecule is held together by covalent bonds.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in O₂ ?
Two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons in a double covalent bond.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in SiO₂ (quartz) ?
Silicon and oxygen are non-metals joined by shared electrons in a giant covalent network.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in an aluminum pop can ?
Aluminum is a metal, so its atoms are held together by a sea of shared, mobile electrons.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in a silver ring ?
Silver atoms in the metal are held together by metallic bonding.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in a gold nugget ?
Gold is a pure metal, so its atoms share a sea of delocalized electrons.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in a zinc strip ?
Zinc is a metal, so metallic bonds hold its atoms together.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in a brass doorknob (copper + zinc) ?
Brass is an alloy of two metals, so its atoms are held by metallic bonds.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in a lump of sodium metal ?
Sodium is a metal; in the pure element its atoms are joined by metallic bonds.
What type of bond holds the atoms together in NO₂ ?
Nitrogen and oxygen are both non-metals, so they share electrons.
sciXsPolyName: What is the name of KNO₂?
NO₂⁻ is the nitrite ion, so KNO₂ is potassium nitrite.
What is the name of Na₂SO₃?
SO₃²⁻ is the sulfite ion, so Na₂SO₃ is sodium sulfite.
What is the name of Ca₃(PO₄)₂?
PO₄³⁻ is the phosphate ion, so the compound is calcium phosphate.
What is the name of LiOH?
OH⁻ is the hydroxide ion, so LiOH is lithium hydroxide.
What is the name of KMnO₄?
MnO₄⁻ is the permanganate ion, so KMnO₄ is potassium permanganate.
What is the name of NaClO₃?
ClO₃⁻ is the chlorate ion, so NaClO₃ is sodium chlorate.
What is the name of NaClO?
ClO⁻ is the hypochlorite ion, so NaClO (found in bleach) is sodium hypochlorite.
What is the name of KClO₄?
ClO₄⁻ is the perchlorate ion, so KClO₄ is potassium perchlorate.
NH₄⁺ is ammonium and SO₄²⁻ is sulfate, giving ammonium sulfate.
What is the name of BaSO₄?
SO₄²⁻ is the sulfate ion, so BaSO₄ is barium sulfate.
What is the name of K₂CrO₄?
CrO₄²⁻ is the chromate ion, so K₂CrO₄ is potassium chromate.
What is the name of K₂Cr₂O₇?
Cr₂O₇²⁻ is the dichromate ion, so K₂Cr₂O₇ is potassium dichromate.
What is the name of NaCH₃COO?
CH₃COO⁻ is the acetate ion, so NaCH₃COO is sodium acetate.
What is the name of NaCN?
CN⁻ is the cyanide ion, so NaCN is sodium cyanide.
What is the name of Ca(OH)₂?
Two OH⁻ hydroxide ions balance Ca²⁺, giving calcium hydroxide.
What is the name of Li₂CO₃?
CO₃²⁻ is the carbonate ion, so Li₂CO₃ is lithium carbonate.
What is the name of NH₄NO₃?
NH₄⁺ is ammonium and NO₃⁻ is nitrate, giving ammonium nitrate.
What is the name of CuSO₄?
SO₄²⁻ has a 2− charge, so copper is Cu²⁺, giving copper(II) sulfate.
What is the name of Fe(OH)₃?
Three OH⁻ ions balance one iron ion, so iron is Fe³⁺: iron(III) hydroxide.
What is the name of Na₃PO₄?
PO₄³⁻ is the phosphate ion, so Na₃PO₄ is sodium phosphate.
What is the name of Mg(NO₃)₂?
NO₃⁻ is the nitrate ion, so Mg(NO₃)₂ is magnesium nitrate.
What is the name of NaHCO₃?
HCO₃⁻ is the hydrogen carbonate ion, so NaHCO₃ (baking soda) is sodium hydrogen carbonate.
sciNameCov: What is the formula for sulfur dioxide ?
"Di" means two, so sulfur dioxide has one sulfur and two oxygen atoms.
What is the formula for dinitrogen monoxide ?
Two nitrogen atoms and one oxygen atom give N₂O.
What is the formula for nitrogen monoxide ?
One nitrogen and one oxygen give NO.
What is the formula for nitrogen dioxide ?
"Dioxide" means two oxygen atoms, giving NO₂.
